title: Venue upgrade latch keys on the ProgramData deploy slot, which a permissionless ExtendProgram rewrites
root_cause: flag_venue_upgraded latches when read_deploy_slot (shortwin-venue-state program_data::deploy_slot, header slot field) differs from the stored guard_slot. The loader's permissionless ExtendProgram rewrites that slot without changing the ELF, so anyone can set the latch and block open_short on every market of the venue. revalidate_venue's require_eq!(slot, expected_slot) has the same slot-only view, so it cannot reliably clear the latch.

members.title: flag_venue_upgraded treats a ProgramData extension as a venue upgrade
Anyone trips the venue latch with a one-byte ExtendProgram
Any caller can set the venue upgrade latch with `ExtendProgram`

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. The issue is reachable by anyone, with one carve-out (pump and pAMM, below).

1. The latch looks only at the slot. flag_venue_upgraded.rs:51 reads the slot through read_deploy_slot (flag_venue_upgraded.rs:44-48). That calls program_data::deploy_slot (crates/shortwin-venue-state/src/program_data.rs:68), which returns u64_at(data, 4), the header slot. At flag_venue_upgraded.rs:67-69 the only condition for setting the bit is `slot != guard_slot`. Neither the ELF nor its length is compared. The accounts struct (lines 22-40) needs no signer. It only checks the address constant and owner == loader, so the caller is anyone.

2. The runtime lets anyone change the slot. The loader's ExtendProgram path (common_extend_program) refuses an extension in the current block or of an immutable program. Otherwise it reallocs, redeploys and writes `ProgramData{slot: clock_slot, ..}` with the ELF unchanged. The project states this is permissionless in its own runtime: docs/audit/known-issues.md:123 (KI-63), ARCHITECTURE §8.5(g), and tests/litesvm/src/squads.rs:646 ("permissionless in Agave 4.2; at least 10 KiB under SIMD-0431"). tests/litesvm/tests/squads_gov_it.rs:864 runs it with a non-authority payer on agave 4.2.2 and follows it with `env.warp(1) // the extension redeployed in its slot`. An attacker can put [ExtendProgram(venue), flag_venue_upgraded(venue)] in one transaction. In addition, the in-house keeper (services/keeper/src/monitor.rs:117-131 latch_action) flags automatically on any slot change. So even a harmless extension, such as a venue team pre-extending before an upgrade, trips the latch.

3. What it blocks. open_short.rs:282, create_market.rs:544 and propose_pool.rs:234 call guard::latch / candidate_latch (engine/guard.rs:110-116). Masks are set in constants.rs:137-145 and state/market.rs:90-98:
   - pfee (index 2) is in both pump masks, so all PumpCurve and PumpSwap opens stop.
   - AMM v4 (3) or CPMM (4) is in GUARD_MASK_RAYDIUM, so all Raydium opens stop.
   Exits are not affected. No funds are at risk; this is a protocol-wide denial of service on opens.

4. Partial refutation, pump and pAMM. Their ProgramData is already 10,485,760 B, the 10 MiB maximum (ARCHITECTURE V9, line 2425). Any ExtendProgram on them fails with InvalidRealloc, so indices 0 and 1 cannot be tripped this way. pfee (948,989 B), AMM v4 (1,406,429 B) and CPMM (793,869 B) are upgradeable (authority set, KI-44/V21) and have room to grow. Tripping those three already covers every enabled venue.

5. Cost. Under SIMD-0431's 10 KiB minimum, each trip costs about 10,240 × 6,960 ≈ 0.071 SOL of rent, locked in the venue's ProgramData, plus fees. Each venue has headroom for roughly 880-940 extensions before reaching 10 MiB, so sustained griefing is bounded but cheap. Without that minimum it is about 7k lamports per trip and effectively unlimited.

6. revalidate_venue (lines 52-53) does exact `require_eq!(slot, expected_slot)`. Once the Emergency stages a Squads proposal (the 2-transaction flow: stage, then approve_and_execute), an attacker who watches for it can extend again so the slot no longer matches. Execution then fails with VenueSlotMismatch, and per KI-63(f) the refused proposal stays Approved but can never succeed. The claim that the latch "cannot be cleared" is overstated. Two Emergency signers can sign stage+approve+execute as one atomic transaction, leaving no window to react. Alternatively, Governance can ship a program upgrade (48 h). So recovery is possible, but it can be griefed and costs a multisig round every time the attacker re-trips.

Severity: Medium. Any unprivileged caller can repeatedly halt all new opens and listings across the pump and Raydium venues for little cost. There is no direct loss of funds.

Prior disclosure: KI-63 / ARCH §8.5(g) disclose permissionless ExtendProgram but call it "harmless", and only in the upgrade context. KI-42 covers latch reaction time. No document discloses that ExtendProgram trips the latch or blocks revalidation, so already_known is empty.

The code confirms the bug. The impact is real, but the reports overstate the cost side and leave out some reach limits.

Mechanism (confirmed):
- The latch reads only the ProgramData header slot: crates/shortwin-venue-state/src/program_data.rs:62/68, then flag_venue_upgraded.rs:51 and :68 `require!(slot != guard_slot)`.
- The loader's ExtendProgram writes `slot: clock_slot` and redeploys the same ELF. The repo acknowledges both: tests/litesvm/tests/squads_gov_it.rs:863-866 (a permissionless extend by a non-authority, then `env.warp(1); // the extension redeployed in its slot`) and tests/litesvm/src/squads.rs:645-647 ("permissionless in Agave 4.2"). LiteSVM 0.16 runs under the mainnet feature set (tokens.rs:4).
- An attacker extends a venue's ProgramData, then calls flag_venue_upgraded. The bit is set and open_short refuses (open_short.rs:282, guard.rs:110).

Corrections to the reports:
1. A one-byte extend does not work. The repo pins a minimum of 10 KiB under SIMD-0431 (squads.rs:646; squads_gov_it.rs:863 `.max(10_240)`). Each trip costs about 10,240 x 6,960 = 71.27M lamports (about 0.071 SOL) of rent plus the fee. That rent is locked in the venue's ProgramData; the attacker cannot get it back.
2. The pump and pAMM ProgramData accounts cannot be extended. They are already 10,485,760 B, which is MAX_PERMITTED_DATA_LENGTH (ARCHITECTURE.md:2425, V9). Reach is still protocol-wide:
   - pfee (948,989 B) is in both GUARD_MASK_PUMP_CURVE and GUARD_MASK_PUMP_SWAP (constants.rs:137-143), so every pump-curve and PumpSwap market can be blocked.
   - Raydium AMM v4 (1,406,429 B) or CPMM (793,869 B) blocks every Raydium market through GUARD_MASK_RAYDIUM. The same latch also blocks Raydium listings in create_market (create_market.rs:544) and pool-selection candidates (propose_pool.rs:234). In execute_pool_switch.rs:170 a latched candidate cancels the fast-path window.
   - The Jupiter bit (index 5) is in no mask, so tripping it does nothing.
   - Each venue can be extended roughly 886-946 times before it hits the 10 MiB cap, about 63-67 SOL to exhaust one venue. The attack is cheap per trip but bounded.
3. Revalidation is not blocked outright. revalidate_venue.rs:53 needs the exact slot, and the Emergency multisig is 2-of-4 with members approving and executing in the Squads app (AUDIT.md:311, 333-335). expected_slot is fixed when the vault transaction is staged. An attacker watching for staged revalidate transactions can re-extend before execution, at about 0.071 SOL per Emergency attempt. When no one front-runs, a revalidation clears the latch normally.
   - The only reliable fix is a program upgrade, which waits for the 48 h Squads time lock (AUDIT.md:310). Expect at least 48 h plus development time of frozen opens across all pump and/or Raydium markets.

What is not affected:
- No funds are lost or frozen. Exits never check the guard (AUDIT.md:138-140). add_margin takes no latch account (add_margin.rs:7, 24-26), so borrowers can still defend positions. Withdrawals are untouched.
- Who loses: traders cannot open new shorts, lenders' idle liquidity earns no new rent, and the protocol loses open fees.
- Secondary effect: a frozen Raydium fast path sends positions on a failed incumbent to S3 at fair value. That is a designed fallback (SPEC.md:333, M4F-1) and needs an independent pool failure first.
- Baseline: pump venues already upgrade several times a month (known-issues.md:111, KI-44), and each upgrade pauses opens until review. The attack turns that bounded pause into one an attacker can extend at will.

Severity: Medium. Any caller can do this cheaply; it repeatedly denies the protocol's main revenue path across every market; only a program upgrade with a 48 h+ time lock fixes it. No principal is at risk, which keeps it below High.

title: vest_in rounds the value-weighted vest end up, so dust sweeps keep pushing vest_end later
root_cause: vest_in computes the new span with mul_div(bal*left + x*lump_vest_s, 1, bal + x, Rounding::Ceil). Any lump, even 1 lamport, against a running vest moves vest_end at least 1 s later. Repeated 1-lamport sweep_trader calls (per second or many in one tx) therefore hold vest_end near now + lump_vest_s, and lenders who exit forfeit the unvested part.

members.title: Repeated 1-lamport sweeps keep moving the vest end later
Many 1-lamport sweeps in one transaction keep moving vest_end later
One-lamport sweeps hold vest_end six hours away

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real, and an anonymous caller can reach it cheaply.

1. The math (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:921-937). Take left = vest_end - now, with left < lump_vest_s. A lump x against a running vest sets span = ceil((bal*left + x*L)/(bal + x)). When x is dust, that is left + 1. When left == L the division is exact and span stays L. So every lump of 1 lamport or more pushes vest_end exactly 1 s later, capped at now + L. vest_in only returns early when lamports == 0 (pool.rs:914). Nothing limits how many lumps land per second, per slot or per transaction.

2. The path. sweep_trader is open to anyone (AUDIT.md:314). Its handler (programs/shortwin/src/instructions/sweep_trader.rs) moves every lamport held by the trader PDA and the trader_wsol PDA into market_vault through normalise_pdas (engine/trader.rs:142-184). It then calls pool::sweep (pool.rs:2106-2126), which calls vest_in with S > 0. Nothing blocks a repeat:
   - no once-per-slot or once-per-transaction guard;
   - no minimum amount;
   - market_now (prologue.rs:55) only clamps time to be non-decreasing.

   The runtime's rent-state check runs before and after the whole transaction, not between instructions. The trader PDA starts and ends at 0 lamports, so it may hold 1 lamport in between. The pattern [System transfer of 1 lamport to the trader PDA, sweep_trader] can therefore repeat many times in one transaction. Several transactions per second (one slot is about 400 ms) work just as well.

3. The impact, from an integer re-implementation of release_in/vest_in. It reproduces the repo's k=60 figure (98.45 % after 6 h, as in pool_econ.rs:207 and lender_it/pot.rs:201). Setup: a 10 SOL lump, then 1-lamport sweeps.
   - One sweep per second, or N sweeps every N seconds (N = 20/30/60): vest_end stays at exactly now + 21,600 s.
   - Released: 63.2 % after 6 h, 98.17 % after 24 h, 99.97 % after 48 h.
   - That is the v0.4 exponential release that R4B-5 says is FIXED (ARCHITECTURE.md:2464; ECONOMICS.md:1345-1354, where v0.4 at k=60 shows 63.3 % / 98.2 %).
   - At 20-30 sweeps per transaction the cost is about 3-4k transactions a day, roughly 0.02 SOL a day plus 1 lamport per sweep.

4. Consequences.
   - KI-09's guidance ("a lender keeps its part by waiting until the market's vest_end") cannot be followed while the griefing runs, because vest_end stays 6 h away indefinitely.
   - A lender who exits after waiting 6 h forfeits about 37 % of its pro-rata share of recent lumps instead of 0. Lumps include penalty halves, expiry fees, S2/S3 premiums and rent top-ups. After 24 h the forfeit is still about 1.8 %.
   - Lenders who deposit after a lump collect part of it, so value shifts from earlier lenders to later ones. A griefer who stays as a lender captures part of what others forfeit.

5. Severity. Low:
   - No protocol insolvency and no theft from the vault. It is a timing and redistribution grief among lenders, bounded by lump sizes.
   - A lender who waits about 24 h still recovers about 98 %.
   - The design rated the original R4B-5 issue LOW.

6. Not refuted. No code blocks repeated dust sweeps. The docs' bound ("a griefer buys at most 1 s per transaction", ARCHITECTURE.md:2464) is wrong when several sweeps run per transaction or several transactions per second. The tests cover only k >= 60 s.

7. Suggested fix. Use Rounding::Floor at pool.rs:937. Floor still never moves the end earlier while L >= left, and a dust lump then moves it 0 s. Alternatively, ignore lumps below a minimum.

Disclosure: the 1 s-per-lump mechanism is documented (ECONOMICS.md:1345; the comment at pool.rs:925-929) and the exit forfeit is KI-09. That a sustained 1 lump per second holds vest_end at now + lump_vest_s and undoes the R4B-5 fix is not disclosed; the docs claim the opposite.

Confirmed. The path is reachable and the claimed impact is right. What it costs lenders is vest yield moving between lenders, not principal.

Mechanism. In crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:924-944, vest_in sets span = ceil((bal*left + x*L)/(bal+x)), and line 937 uses Rounding::Ceil. Take x = 1 with 0 < L - left <= bal + 1. That expression equals left + (L-left)/(bal+1), so the ceiling gives left + 1, and vest_end moves exactly 1 s later. A second call in the same transaction runs release_in (pool.rs:856-879) with now == vest_last, which releases nothing, so each call adds another 1 s. The push stops only when vest_end reaches now + lump_vest_s (21,600 s by default; at most 604,800 s, ARCH:471).

Reachability. sweep_trader is permissionless (sweep_trader.rs:1-4, 'anyone'). It moves any balance of the trader PDA, with no minimum (trader.rs:281-305; normalise_pdas at sweep_trader.rs:~244), into pool::sweep -> vest_in (sweep_trader.rs:335; pool.rs:2106-2125). So an attacker can send pairs of [system transfer 1 lamport to the trader PDA, sweep_trader], several per transaction. A small program of the attacker's own can also loop this through CPI, so the 1.4M compute-unit budget limits it rather than transaction size. Rent is checked once per transaction, and the PDA ends each one at 0 lamports.

Quantified impact. I checked this with an exact integer copy of release_in and vest_in: a 10 SOL lump, then 1-lamport sweeps. With a sweep every 60 s, 98.4% is released after 6 h, which matches ECON's table. With sweeps every 1 s, or batched 20 or 25 per transaction, vest_end - now stays at 21,600 s. Release then decays exponentially with a time constant of 6 h:
- 39.3% released after 3 h
- 63.2% after 6 h
- 86.5% after 12 h
- 98.2% after 24 h
- about 99.97% after 48 h
This is exactly the v0.4 behaviour (63.3% after 6 h) that R4B-5 was meant to remove (ECONOMICS.md:35, :1345-1354).

Who loses. A lender that exits at the nominal 6 h end forfeits 36.8% of its pro-rata share of the lump instead of 0%, and at 3 h it forfeits 60.7% instead of 50%. The forfeited SOL goes to the lenders who stay (ECON:1356, KI-09). KI-09's mitigation, 'wait until the market's vest_end' (docs/audit/known-issues.md:55), stops working, because vest_end stays 6 h away for as long as the attack runs.

Cost to the attacker. It pays 1 lamport per second pushed, plus fees. At 20-40 sweeps per transaction that is about 0.01-0.02 SOL per day in base fees. Sending one transaction per second costs about 0.43 SOL per day. No priority fee is needed, because the attacker can catch up later.

Why only Low:
- No principal is lost and the pool stays solvent; only lump, premium and top-up vest moves between lenders.
- A lender can recover nearly all of it by waiting 24-48 h, at a cost in time and token exposure.
- The attacker profits only through its own shares, when others exit early. For example, a 50% stayer collects about 1.84 SOL of a 10 SOL lump from a 50% lender that leaves at 6 h.
- Lumps can still be large (ECON's S2/S3 table shows 27.85-112 SOL premiums), so the loss to one lender can be material.

Fix. Rounding::Floor keeps the 'never earlier' property while lump_vest_s >= left, because floor((bal*left + x*L)/(bal+x)) >= left. With floor, a dust lump no longer moves the end.

Disclosure. This exact attack is not disclosed. ECON R4B-5 states 'a dust lump by at most 1 s (the ceiling)' but tests only sweeps every 60 s or slower, and claims the attack is fixed. KI-09 discloses the forfeit but relies on vest_end as the escape.

title: lender_credit floors each accrual's rent credit and carries no remainder
root_cause: rent::lender_credit returns dot_div(aggr.a, delta, 1, RENT_DEN_BPS, Floor). prologue::accrue calls it on every accrual and keeps no remainder. Frequent cranks (crank_price every second) floor each small credit to 0, and the true-up still removes the exact share, so lenders permanently lose up to a lamport per accrual.

members.title: accrue floors each lender rent credit and keeps no remainder
accrue floors each lender rent credit and drops the remainder
lender_credit drops its remainder, so lenders lose rent on every accrual

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real and anyone can trigger it, but it is capped at under 1 lamport per market per second.

How it happens:
- crates/shortwin-math/src/rent.rs:373-374: lender_credit = dot_div(aggr.a, delta, 1, RENT_DEN_BPS, Floor). No remainder is stored in the Market or the Pool.
- programs/shortwin/src/engine/prologue.rs:89-101: accrue books that floored credit through pool::accrue (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:2083-2097). That adds it to receivable and to the entitlement `acc` via credit_in. The fraction cut off is dropped.

The close does not give it back:
- At close, credited = credited_for, which rounds up the position's exact share (rent.rs:357-366).
- close_pos (pool.rs:2160-2167) takes min(credited, receivable) off receivable.
- true_up (pool.rs:2187-2205): top = lender_rent − credited (rent_top_up) goes to the vest. The entitlement change is immediate − credited, which is 0 whenever lender_rent ≥ credited, and that is always the case because lender_rent ≥ the exact share. Realised SOL `acc_r` gets credited.
- So lenders are entitled to (sum of floors) + (lender_rent − ⌈exact⌉) in total. That is less than the lender_rent paid into lender_sol by ⌈exact⌉ − sum of floors. The gap is up to 1 lamport per accrual, plus up to 1 per position.
- The extra realised SOL becomes surplus on each lender (realised minus claimed above `pending`). to_pot (pool.rs:1540-1547) moves it to `unmatched`. claim (pool.rs:2007-2036) never pays a lender more than its `pending` entitlement, and pot draws are limited to the lender's own deficit. So the gap stays in the vault, owned by no one. ECON §9.6 (line 1466) only describes this kind of leftover as "rounding".

Who can trigger it:
- crank_price (programs/shortwin/src/instructions/crank_price.rs:1-4, 59-80) needs no signer. So do the other Market-writing instructions. Each one runs the prologue's accrual.
- Two accruals in the same second have dt = 0, so the delta is 0 (rent.rs:258-262). The worst case is therefore one floored accrual per market per second.
- The keeper itself cranks every second near thresholds and every 30 s when idle (ARCH line 1893).

Size of the loss:
- At most under 1 lamport per market-second: about 86,400 lamports a day, about 0.03 SOL a year per market.
- On small markets the share of rent lost can be large. Example: 1 SOL notional at 10% a year with a 15% protocol share credits lenders about 2.69 lamports a second. Cranked every second, about 0.69 of that (about 26%) is lost. If the market's total credit is under 1 lamport a second, all of it is lost.
- An attacker gains nothing. Each crank costs at least a 5,000-lamport fee (a batched crank still costs hundreds of lamports per market) to destroy under 1 lamport.

Why Low and not higher: the loss is a tiny, griefing-only leak with no profit for anyone. It mirrors the accepted per-touch floor in KI-68.
verdicts.already_known: Partly. The rounding choice is on purpose and documented: floor the aggregate at each accrual, round up per position at the true-up, so that receivable returns to 0 (I-P7). See ECON §7 (docs/design/ECONOMICS.md:1048-1052), ARCH §4.5 (docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:1535-1540) and the comment at rent.rs:350-353. ECON §9.6 (line 1466) calls the wind-down leftover "rounding". No known-issues entry measures the resulting lender loss of up to 1 lamport per accrual. KI-68 (docs/audit/known-issues.md:67) discloses only the similar per-touch floor on lender accrual.

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real. The impact is rounding dust: it is systematic, but small in absolute terms and nobody profits from it.

**How the code loses the value**
- `rent::lender_credit` (crates/shortwin-math/src/rent.rs:373-374) floors each accrual's aggregate credit and keeps no remainder.
- `prologue::accrue` (programs/shortwin/src/engine/prologue.rs:99-100) passes that floored value to `pool::accrue`, which adds it to `receivable` and `acc` (pool.rs:2081-2096). There is no carry field. This is unlike the `acc` division itself, which keeps `carry` (ECON §2.1).
- At exit, `credited` is `rent::credited_for`: the exact, ceiled amount for the position's whole life, not the sum of the floored credits (engine/waterfall.rs:99, instructions/sol_settle.rs:265).
- The true-up (pool.rs:2186-2205) computes `top = rent_top_up(lender_rent, lender_rent, credited) = max(0, lender_rent - credited)`. It then adds `immediate - credited` (0 when the rent covers it) to `acc` and adds `immediate = credited` to `acc_r`. Because the top-up is measured against the exact amount, it never gives back the floored-away units.
- Result: all of `lender_rent` enters `lender_sol` (pool.rs:2245), but entitlement holds only the floored sum plus the top-up. Realised SOL therefore exceeds entitlement by (`credited_for` - the floored credits). That surplus goes to the pot `unmatched` at the lender's next touch (pool.rs:1267). Claims are capped by `pending`, so the gap stays in `lender_sol` and no one can claim it.
- Who loses: the lenders. No attacker or the protocol gains anything.

**How much**
- **Per accrual:** the loss is `frac(c)`, under 1 lamport, where `c` is the aggregate lender credit since the last accrual.
- **At most one lossy accrual per second per market:** `dt` is whole seconds, and when `dt = 0` the change in `J` is 0 (rent.rs:258-262).
- **Upper bound per market:** under 86,400 lamports per day (0.0000864 SOL), or under about 0.0078 SOL over a 90-day maximum duration.
- **Relative loss:** `frac(c)/c`. It is only large when the market's aggregate open interest is tiny.
  - Example: one 0.1 SOL minimum-notional position (G26) on Tier A at 15% APR, lender share 85%, gives c ≈ 0.40 lamports/s. Under per-second cranks every credit floors to 0, so lenders lose 100% of the continuous rent: about 34,900 lamports per day, about 0.0031 SOL over 90 days.
  - The same position at the 30 s idle cadence (ECON §5.8, duty 1) has c ≈ 12.1 per accrual: about 1.1% lost, about 370 lamports per day.
  - 1 SOL at 15% under per-second cranks: c ≈ 4.04, about 1% lost.
  - 10 SOL at 50%: c ≈ 135 per second, about 0.4% or less lost.
- **Griefing:** `crank_price` is permissionless, but each transaction costs a 5,000-lamport fee to destroy under 1 lamport. It is uneconomic, and the attacker gains nothing.

**Design intent**
- The floor is the normative design, not a slip:
  - ECON §2.1 numerics row "lender rent credit" (ECONOMICS.md:250).
  - ECON §7 (lines 1048 and 1052): "each accrual floors the aggregate while each true-up ceils per position" so that `receivable` never goes negative and I-P7 holds.
  - ARCH lines 1535 and 1540.
- I-P6 (ECONOMICS.md:3464) accepts "rounding" dust left in `lender_sol`.
- ECON line 149 and changelog line 3828 mention "≤ 1 lamport per accrual" rounding.
- What the docs never say is that these per-accrual floors add up, or that per-second cranks can wipe all continuous rent in markets with small open interest.

**Fix**
Carrying the remainder (as `acc` already does) would close it. `receivable` would still stay at or below Σ`credited_for`.

**Severity**
Fair severity is Low: the leak is real and systematic but dust-level, and nobody can profit from it.
verdicts.already_known:
Partly. The floor is the specified design and only its rounding is acknowledged; the cumulative loss is not disclosed:
- ECONOMICS.md:250 (§2.1 numerics row "lender rent credit")
- ECONOMICS.md §7, lines 1048 and 1052
- ARCHITECTURE.md:1535 and 1540 (floor the aggregate, ceil the true-up)
- I-P6 (ECONOMICS.md:3464) accepts rounding dust in `lender_sol`
- ECONOMICS.md:149 and 3828 mention "≤ 1 lamport per accrual" rounding

No entry in docs/AUDIT.md or docs/audit/known-issues.md covers the cumulative per-accrual loss. KI-68, the per-touch floor on the lender side, is the closest analogue and is accepted, but it is a different code path.

title: apply_config installs new governance/pause keys without their signatures
root_cause: For ConfigChange::Authorities, apply_config checks only fee_recipient, and GlobalConfig::apply writes governance and pause_authority (and coverage_authority) directly. Neither requires the new keys to sign nor uses a two-step accept, so one mistyped key loses that role, and with it every later config change, for good.

members.title: apply_config installs a new governance key that never signs
apply_config installs a new governance key without its signature

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real, but the impact in the report is overstated.

What the code does:
- `GlobalConfig::apply` (programs/shortwin/src/state/config.rs:187-196) writes `governance`, `pause_authority`, `coverage_authority` and `fee_recipient` directly from the pending change.
- The only checks on the new keys are in `check_authorities` (config.rs:766-794). It rejects a default key for governance, pause authority and fee recipient, and it requires the four keys to be pairwise distinct (SQ-G8). It never asks the new key to prove it can sign.
- `apply_config` (programs/shortwin/src/instructions/apply_config.rs:85-97) takes an extra account only for `fee_recipient`, and only checks that it is System-owned and not executable (`check_fee_recipient`, config.rs:815-822). The new `governance` and `pause_authority` never sign, and there is no second accept step.
- `propose_config` (propose_config.rs:19-25) is signed only by the current governance.
- So a key that is valid but nobody controls passes `propose_config` and later the permissionless `apply_config`. The only actor who can trigger this is Governance itself, a 3-of-5 multisig, by mistake.

Why "lost for good" is wrong:
1. The program's upgrade authority is a separate setting held by Governance vault 0 (AUDIT.md:297 and :309; SPEC.md:280), and an `Authorities` change does not touch it. If `config.governance` is set to a wrong key, the same multisig can still upgrade the program after its 48 h Squads time lock and restore the config.
2. A wrong `pause_authority` or `coverage_authority` does not lock anything up. Governance keeps its role and fixes it with another timelocked `Authorities` change. The Emergency clear also covers coverage, per SPEC.md:278. Only a wrong `governance` field freezes later config changes, and only until that upgrade.

Why it is unlikely to happen:
- The change must pass a 3-of-5 approval, the 48 h Squads time lock and the 48 h program timelock, and `ConfigProposed` is emitted on chain.
- The staging tool `stage-authorities` (services/ops/src/cli.rs:508-537) does not take hand-typed keys. It derives all four from the multisig layout (`Layout::authorities`, services/ops/src/config.rs:300-307) and prints the diff. It also only stages through the layout's own multisigs (`governing_ms`), so it never moves governance to an arbitrary key.

What makes it worse:
- KI-61 discloses that nobody can cancel an `Authorities` change in time. The Emergency cannot cancel it (cancel_config.rs:16-17, 40-44), and Governance's own cancel lands at `not_before` at the earliest, racing `apply_config`. A typo caught during the window is therefore hard to stop on chain, but the upgrade path above still recovers it.

Severity: Informational. It is a missing two-step handover for a trusted multisig's own mistake, and it can be recovered through the upgrade authority. At most it is Low as a hardening item.
verdicts.already_known: Not disclosed as such. docs/audit/known-issues.md KI-61 (line 121) only says no one can cancel a pending Authorities change in time. config.rs:755-756 explains that the zero-key check exists because a default key could never sign. Neither covers a non-default key that nobody controls, or a two-step accept.

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real, but the claimed impact ("loses that role ... for good") is overstated.

What the code does (confirmed):
- `GlobalConfig::apply` (programs/shortwin/src/state/config.rs:187-196) writes `governance`, `pause_authority` and `coverage_authority` directly from the payload.
- The only checks are `check_authorities` (config.rs:766-794): the keys must be non-zero and pairwise distinct (SQ-G8).
- `apply_config.rs:85-97` also checks the new `fee_recipient` account: it must match the payload, be System-owned and not executable.
- No new key signs and there is no accept step. `apply_config` is permissionless (AUDIT.md:316).
- A 3-of-5 Governance proposal with a wrong `governance` key would install it once the timelock runs. From then on, `propose_config` (propose_config.rs:25), Governance's `cancel_config` and Governance's admin actions are dead.

Why the impact is much smaller than claimed:
1. **Not "for good".** The `shortwin` upgrade authority is Governance vault 0 (AUDIT.md:297, 309). It lives in the loader's ProgramData, not in `GlobalConfig.governance`, so a bad config key does not touch it. Vault 0 can ship a recovery upgrade after its 48 h Squads time lock. No program timelock applies to upgrades (AUDIT.md:319; ARCH.md:2118 (d)). The worst case is a temporary freeze of governance-only config changes: about 48 h plus development time.
2. **No funds at risk.** Governance cannot move funds (AUDIT.md:310). Closes, liquidations, withdrawals, claims and settlements do not need it. While Governance is out, the Emergency vault keeps `set_pause`, `disable_venue`, `set_route_broken` and `set_venue_extras`.
3. **The other roles are not a "for good" loss either.** A wrong `pause_authority` or `coverage_authority` is rotated by the still-working Governance with a new `Authorities` change. The cost is about 96 h without the fast Emergency path (Governance's own `set_pause` waits on its 48 h Squads time lock). A stray coverage pause can still be undone, since Emergency clears coverage pauses whether or not the role is installed (config.rs:124-126).
4. **The typo has to get past 3-of-5 multisig review and about 96 h of public visibility:**
   - 48 h Squads time lock, during which members can cancel the vault proposal (`shortwin-gov cancel`);
   - then 48 h `timelock_s`.
   - `shortwin-gov verify` WARNs on any pending config change and says whether it matches the layout (services/ops/src/verify.rs:17-18).
   - It FAILs if a multisig PDA does not exist (verify.rs:6-8).
5. **The supported tool cannot hand-type these keys.** `stage-authorities` derives every authority from the layout's verified multisigs (services/ops/src/config.rs:300-307). It can only propose through the multisig whose vault 0 is already `governance`, and it explicitly does not support moving governance to another multisig (services/ops/src/cli.rs:539-552). In practice it never changes `governance` at all.
6. **A wrong but live key is mostly blocked.** SQ-G8 refuses reusing the Emergency vault or the fee vault (config.rs:766-794). Another vault index of the same Squads multisig would still be controlled by it.

Residual: a hand-built Governance proposal with a mistyped key, approved by 3 of 5 and not cancelled in time. Nobody can cancel an `Authorities` change reactively (KI-61), and `propose_config` would replace a pending change but also lands only after the Squads time lock. Even then the result is a temporary freeze of governance-only actions, fixed by an upgrade. No user loses lamports or tokens.

Fair severity: Informational, as a two-step-acceptance hardening note.
verdicts.already_known: Partly. docs/audit/known-issues.md KI-61 (and AUDIT.md:323-325, ARCH.md:2118 (c)) disclose that nobody can cancel a pending `Authorities` change in time: Governance's cancel lands at `not_before` at the earliest, racing `apply_config`. The design also acknowledges a key that can never sign "would freeze the config", but guards only against the zero key (config.rs:762-763). The missing signature or accept step for new governance and pause keys is not listed as a known issue.

title: rewards_required reads the current venue kind, so the full-wipe cashback gate drops after a market leaves pump
root_cause: lender::rewards_required returns true only while market.venue_kind() is PumpCurve/PumpMigrating/PumpSwap. deposit passes it to deposit_in, and sweep_trader uses the same test. Once a wiped curve market moves to None (or Raydium), the WIPE_REWARDS_CLAIMED requirement disappears, so a depositor ends the live wipe record before the curve-era cashback in the pump UVA is swept, and new lenders take it.

members.title: deposit drops the cashback gate after a curve market leaves pump
A deposit ends the full-wipe record before the curve cashback arrives

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real, and the stated actor (any depositor) can reach it. Nothing in the code blocks the path, but it only opens after a rare external event, and the amount at stake is small.

Code path:
(1) `rewards_required` (engine/lender.rs:185-190) reads the market's current `venue_kind()` and returns true only for PumpCurve, PumpMigrating and PumpSwap. `deposit` passes it straight to `pool::deposit` (instructions/deposit.rs:141). When the gate is false, `deposit_in` (shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1939-1949) requires only WIPE_TRADER_SWEPT, then sets `wipe_live = 0`, which finalises the wipe record.
(2) A curve market can leave the pump kinds. `pump_curve::sync` (venues/pump_curve.rs:597-628) moves PumpCurve or PumpMigrating to None and sets `graduated_elsewhere` when the curve has completed with vT == 0 and no canonical pool exists. A None market can later adopt a Raydium pool. No production path sets a pump kind back except the None→pump re-detection.
(3) On a None or Raydium market, `sweep_trader` treats the market as non-pump (sweep_trader.rs:173-176). It passes no token leg and never reads the pump UVA, so `rewards_clear` is false. It still sets the trader bit even when nothing moves.
(4) Curve-era cashback stays in the trader's pump UVA (`market.pump_uva`) until someone calls pump's permissionless `claim_cashback`. That cashback is 30 bps on legacy cashback coins (research/pumpfun-bonding-curve.md:591, 801). The UVA is per user, not per coin, so it stays claimable after the curve migrates elsewhere.
(5) `sol_settle` is permissionless (the `keeper` signer can be anyone, sol_settle.rs:96) and is the only settlement on a None market (S3).

Attack: an attacker bundles [sol_settle (the last S3 settlement, with T = 0, rolls a full wipe), sweep_trader, deposit]. Alternatively, they back-run the settlement before the keeper's post-wipe bundle lands. The deposit passes because only the trader bit is needed, and it ends the wipe record. Any later [claim_cashback, sweep_trader] then runs with S > 0, so the cashback vests over `lump_vest_s` to the new lenders (sweep_trader.rs:303-305, 340-342) instead of topping up the wiped epoch's record.

The keeper does not protect against this. Its `wipe_pending` mirrors the same venue test. Its post-wipe bundle does prepend a pump claim on any market with claimable UVA lamports, but only if that bundle lands first, which the attacker preempts.

The M6-SEC-5 fix and its comment (lender.rs:174-178) show the developers treat this leak as a bug, but the fix covered only PumpMigrating.

Why Low:
- The transition to None needs pump itself to change its migration target. No attacker can cause it.
- Cashback only accrues on deprecated legacy cashback coins, at 30 bps of the trader's curve volume.
- The keeper's duty 13 claims cashback weekly once it reaches 0.01 SOL, so at most about a week of curve-era accrual is exposed.
- A full wipe (T + ΣB_Q = 0) must happen on that market while the cashback is still unclaimed.
- The loss is that bounded cashback, moved from the wiped lenders to new depositors. No principal is at risk.

The code path is real. The impact is a small, conditional loss of value from the wiped epoch's lenders to new depositors. No principal is at risk.

Mechanism (verified):
- `engine/lender.rs:185-190`: `rewards_required` looks only at the current `venue_kind()`.
- `instructions/deposit.rs:134-142` passes that value to `pool::deposit`.
- `shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1939-1951`: when S==0 and `wipe_live`, only `WIPE_TRADER_SWEPT` is needed if `rewards_required` is false. The deposit then clears `wipe_live`, which makes the record final.

Ways a market can leave the pump kinds:
- `venues/pump_curve.rs:597-631` (`sync`): a curve that is complete, with no canonical pool and vT==0, moves PumpCurve or PumpMigrating to None and sets `GRADUATED_ELSEWHERE`.
- `propose_pool` can then adopt a Raydium pool.
- PumpSwap never leaves, because `sync` only handles the curve kinds and `propose_pool` refuses pump venues. So the only exit is curve to None, and possibly on to Raydium.

Why the gate disappears:
- On None, `sweep_trader` (`sweep_trader.rs:165-200`) takes no token leg and never reads the pump UVA. It sets only the trader bit.
- The cashback is still reachable. `Market.pump_uva` sits in the curve cache (`state/market.rs:314`), not in the `pool_cache` union, so it survives the move to None and to Raydium. Pump's `claim_cashback(user = trader)` is permissionless and does not depend on the venue.
- After the deposit, S>0, so a later claim plus sweep vests the cashback over `lump_vest_s` to the new shares (ARCH §3.3 line 1082).

Two orders lead here:
- (a) Wipe on the curve, rewards bit still clear, then the move to None. This needs the keeper's post-wipe bundle to have failed.
- (b) Move to None with positions open, S3 after `s3_wait_s` = 600 s (ECON:3569), a full wipe on None, and then a deposit. This order is the more natural one.

The worst case brings back R4A-7. `sol_settle` lets anyone act as keeper (`sol_settle.rs:6`). An attacker can land `[sol_settle (wiping), sweep_trader, deposit(dust)]` in one transaction, then `[claim_cashback, sweep_trader]`. They take the vest over 6 h. On a no-route None market few others deposit, so they are likely to get nearly all of it.

Quantification:
- Only legacy cashback coins are affected. Pump stopped allowing new cashback coins on 2026-09-12 (`docs/research/pumpfun-bonding-curve.md:56,591`).
- Cashback is 30 bps of the trader PDA's curve trade volume (`pumpfun-bonding-curve.md:801`).
- Only cashback outstanding at the wipe is lost. Cashback claimed while S>0 already vested to the same lenders.
- The keeper's duty 13 claims at most weekly, and only once claimable cashback reaches 0.01 SOL (`cashback_interval_s` 604,800, `cashback_min_lamports` 10,000,000; ECON:3630-3631). The outstanding amount is therefore below 0.01 SOL, or up to about one week of curve-era accrual. That is about 0.03 SOL per 10 SOL of trader volume, so typically 0.01 to a few tenths of a SOL per event.

Mitigations, none enforced on chain:
- The keeper's `sweep::claim_ixs` and `post_wipe_ixs` (`services/keeper/src/sweep.rs:307-343`, `keeper.rs:1888-1934`) read `market.pump_uva` on any venue. So an honest post-wipe bundle on None also claims the pump cashback first. A depositor or attacker has to get in ahead of it.

Likelihood is low:
- The move to None needs pump to change its migration target, which is an external event. Today's `migrate_v2` leads to PumpSwap, which keeps the gate.
- The market must be a legacy cashback coin.
- The pool must be fully wiped (T = 0 when the last borrowed tokens settle).

Docs:
- ARCH §3.3 (line 1046) requires the bit only "on a pump venue that can execute".
- ECON §9.5 (line 1438) says a venue that cannot execute does not block deposits, because "nothing can be claimed from it then". That premise is false for the pump UVA under the as-built claim-then-sweep pattern.
- M6-SEC-5 fixed the PumpMigrating version of this exact problem, for the same reason (`lender.rs:166-170`). So this outcome goes against the stated R4A-7 goal and is not an intended design choice.
- The None/Raydium case is not in `docs/audit/known-issues.md` or in AUDIT.md.

Severity is Low: a bounded amount of SOL moves from the wiped epoch's lenders to new depositors, and only under rare preconditions.

title: The min_notional floor admits positions whose fixed K_s + ert leave no buyback room at the liquidation boundary
root_cause: Params bounds MinNotional at (10_000_000, ..). At that floor, V at CR = cr_liq cannot cover B̂ + ert + K_s, because K_s has a fixed part (risk::k_s). risk::buyback_allowed (B̂_live + ert ≤ V − K_s) is then always false, so liquidate/expire refuse with UseSolSettle and the only exit is S1, which pays lenders V − K_s and the keeper a large share of the vault. open_short does not check this either.

members.title: open_short accepts small shorts that no keeper can liquidate
A fixed K_s reserve blocks every buyback at the legal min_notional floor

verdicts.reason:
The arithmetic is real, but it only happens after governance lowers min_notional. It cannot happen at the default.

**What the code does**
- params.rs:998 bounds min_notional to [10,000,000, 1,000,000,000] lamports. check_econ (params.rs:1206-1240) only range-checks it. No rule ties it to K_s, ert or the tier CRs, and sim/config_check.py does not model min_notional, so the CI gate cannot catch a bad value either.
- open_short.rs:520-541 checks only `n_open >= min_notional` and the market notional cap. At :543 V = S + M = ceil(cr_open * max(B_spot, B_ema)). Nothing checks that the position is affordable to buy back at cr_liq.
- K_s = min(fixed + 1% of V, cap, V) (risk.rs:400-407). Default fixed = 10,000,000 (0.01 SOL); compiled max is also 0.01 SOL (params.rs:963).
- liquidate.rs:331-376 builds Budget{v: pos.v, k_s, ert}. At :435/:448 liquidate and expire refuse with UseSolSettle unless `B_live + ert <= V - K_s` (risk.rs:103-112, 263-270).
- settle.rs:124-135 uses the same test as the S1 legs, and evaluate (settle.rs:556-601) runs S1 when the position is cr_liquidatable or expired, after 40 EMA updates. So the position never gets stuck; it always ends in S1. Lenders get V - K_s and the borrower gets nothing (ECON §8.6).

**Worked numbers at min_notional = 0.01 SOL**
- **Tier A:** N_open = 10M, so V >= 20M and K_s = 10.2M, leaving room = 9.8M. Even at the open price, B_live of about 10M is above that room. At the cr_liq boundary B is about 16M. Liquidation goes to S1: lenders get 9.8M against tokens worth about 16M (about −39%), and the keeper takes 51% of V. The borrower's margin M = 10M is less than K_s = 10.2M. A borrower who wins the sol_settle race as keeper therefore gets the margin back, which is close to a free option paid for by lenders.
- **Tier B:** room 14.75M < B 18.5M.
- **Tier C:** room 19.7M < B 20M.
- **Tier D:** buyback still fits up to ert of about 6.7M; it fails near the 10M ert cap.

The claim that the check is "always false" is slightly overstated. It is false at the liquidation boundary. At expiry it can pass if the price has fallen (on Raydium a drop of about 2% is enough).

**Why it does not happen at defaults**
The default min_notional is 100,000,000 (params.rs:189). Tier A then has V >= 0.2 SOL, room 0.188 SOL, and B + ert at the boundary is at most 0.16 + 0.01. That holds even with KI-12's 9% undercut of min_notional.

For Tier A, the problem starts once min_notional is below about:
- 0.026 SOL on Raydium (ert = 0);
- 0.043 SOL on pump venues at the default ert of 6.5M;
- 0.053 SOL with ert and the fixed keeper fee both at their caps.

**Who can trigger it**
Only governance (3-of-5 multisig, about 96 hours of timelocks) choosing a value inside the compiled bounds, or the deployer at initialize_config. After that, any borrower can open such positions and any keeper can settle them through S1.

**Severity**
Low. It is a missing relational check in config validation. The lender loss is bounded per position (about 0.006 SOL each at the floor), but it adds up across many positions and creates a borrower free option.

The code path is real, but it only appears after governance moves min_notional down from its default. It is not reachable with the default configuration.

**Code path**
- params.rs:998 allows MinNotional down to 10^7.
- open_short.rs:521-527 only checks n_open >= min_notional. V = s + m (line 576), which is about cr_open·N.
- risk.rs:400-407 sets K_s = min(fixed + 1%·V, cap, V), with fixed = 10^7 by default (params.rs:177).
- risk.rs:263-270 / 103-111: a buyback needs B̂_live + ert <= V − K_s. Here ert = exec_rent_tol (6.5·10^6) on PumpCurve and PumpSwap and 0 on other venues (venues/mod.rs:1197-1201).
- When that fails, liquidate.rs:435 and 448 revert with UseSolSettle for both liquidate and expire.
- The only exit left is S1: s1_legs (settle.rs:125-136), and S1 pays lenders V − K_s, the borrower 0 and the keeper K_s (settle.rs:647-656).
- The borrower's own close_short has no K_s gate.

**Quantified at N = 10^7 with default tiers and keeper terms**
- Tier A on PumpSwap: V = 2.0e7, K_s = 1.02e7 (51% of V), room = 3.3e6. A buyback needs CR >= 6.06, which is never true after open (CR_open is 2.0).
- Tier A on Raydium: room = 9.8e6, so a buyback needs CR >= 2.04. That fails even at open, and at expiry unless the price fell.
- Tier B fails at cr_liq on both venues. Tier C fails at cr_liq on both venues; on Raydium the miss is narrow (room 19.7e6 against B̂ 20.0e6).
- Tier D works at the floor (pump room 2.31e7 against B̂_liq 2.286e7). The claim "every buyback" is therefore overstated: it holds for A, B and C only.

**Who loses**
- At the Tier A liquidation boundary (B̂ = 1.6e7), S1 pays keeper 10,200,000, lenders 9,800,000 and borrower 0.
- A buyback liquidation would have given lenders Q (about 1.6e7) plus a 4e5 penalty share. The keeper would have got about 3.4e6 (penalty share plus a floor top-up capped by the remainder), and the borrower 0.
- Net effect: about 6.7e6 lamports (about 0.0067 SOL, roughly 40% of the lender claim) moves from lenders to the keeper per position.
- At expiry with the price unchanged (Tier A, pump), a normal expire would return about 8.8e6 − R_due to the borrower. S1 gives the borrower 0, so the borrower loses nearly the whole margin unless they close_short before the deadline. Lenders get 9.8e6, which is below the token value plus fee plus rent.
- If the borrower is also the keeper, K_s (about the borrower's margin) comes back to them in every S1, so the margin stops protecting lenders.
- Each position is at most about 0.01 SOL. Losses per market are bounded by market_max_notional (default 25 SOL).

**Where it starts and why it is Low**
Minimum safe N, by tier (Raydium / PumpSwap):
- A: 2.63e7 / 4.34e7 (5.26e7 with exec_rent_tol at its maximum)
- B: 1.60e7 / 2.65e7
- C: 1.03e7 / 1.70e7
- D: safe at the floor

The default min_notional of 1e8 (params.rs:189) leaves a band down to CR of about 1.06-1.10, so the default configuration is unaffected. Triggering the issue needs the trusted 3-of-5 governance to approve an in-bounds min_notional below these values, behind a 96-hour timelock. That trust requirement and the small absolute size per position are why this is Low.

It is still a bounds-derivation flaw:
- ECON §5.7 / #77 (ECONOMICS.md:28, 617, 648) says that compiled bounds of parameters that affect liveness were re-derived so no in-bounds value loses liquidations. It notes that small positions are S1-prone through K_s's fixed part.
- ARCH §2.3.3 (ARCHITECTURE.md:431) says the simulator does not model min_notional. So params::validate_econ and the config_check.py liveness gate would both pass a floor value.
verdicts.already_known:
Not disclosed as such. Related but different items:
- KI-12 (known-issues.md:58): a sale-wrapped open can undercut min_notional by about 9%.
- ECONOMICS.md:1130 / R3B-10: small positions rely on the in-house keeper. This is about keeper incentives, covered by the liquidation keeper floor.
- ECONOMICS.md:617 and 648: generic notes that small positions are S1-prone through K_s's fixed part, and that keeper terms are capped for that reason.

No doc says that the compiled min_notional floor of 10^7 removes buyback entirely for Tiers A-C.

title: maybe_roll_in flushes the unreleased vest only on a full wipe, not on a rebase roll
root_cause: maybe_roll_in pays vest_bal to the old shares only when token_claims() == 0. A dust deposit made before the last settlement leaves claims > 0, so the epoch rolls as a 1/1000^k rebase instead. vest_bal stays pending and is later released to post-rebase shares, which a dust depositor holds almost entirely.

members.title: A rebase roll leaves the unreleased vest to a dust depositor
A dust deposit before the last settlement skips the full-wipe vest flush

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real, and the stated actor can reach it.

Code path:
- settle (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:2273-2302) vests the last settlement's lump and rent top-up at :2290 before maybe_roll_in runs at :2291.
- maybe_roll_in (:2311-2330) flushes vest_bal to the old shares only in the `claims == 0` branch (:2316-2324).
- When claims > 0 it either does not roll or rebases by 1/1000^k (:2326-2335). vest_bal stays where it is, and release_in (:857-890) later pays it out pro rata to whoever then holds shares.
- The program adds no dust handling. sol_settle.rs:268 calls pool::settle as is, and its signer is "anyone" (sol_settle.rs:5).

The attacker's deposit is open to anyone:
- The only checks are amount > 0 at deposit.rs:104, the mint guard, and minted > 0 (pool.rs deposit_in :1923-1956).
- A deposit mints at (S+VS)/(T+ΣB_Q+VA) (shares_for_tokens :1668). Shares per token only rise, so 1 raw token always mints shares.
- With T=0 and ΣB_Q>0, util_ok (caps.rs:163; util_cap_bps 9,000, at most 9,500) blocks any open from borrowing that token back, so the dust stays in T.
- The attacker can also bundle [deposit(1), sol_settle, deposit(X)] itself, since sol_settle is permissionless.

After the settlement the token claims are 1 raw unit:
- The old lenders' post-rebase shares are backed by about 1 token.
- A newcomer's X tokens mint about X/(X+2) of S, and that position collects that fraction of the remaining vest over lump_vest_s.

I ran the repo's parity model (docs/design/sim/pool_model.py, imported read-only from the scratchpad; the repo is unmodified). Setup: two lenders with 10^12 tokens, all of it lent out (or lent to the 90% cap with every free token then withdrawn), then a final settlement of 50 SOL with a 5 SOL lump.
- **No attack:** the roll is a full wipe and the lenders are paid 50,000,000,000 lamports.
- **1 raw token deposited before the settlement:** the roll becomes a rebase of 1/10^9 with vest_bal 5,000,000,000 left in place. The attacker then deposits 10^6 raw tokens and waits about 6 h. It is paid 4,999,990,010 lamports and gets its tokens back (999,999 of 1,000,001). The lenders are paid 45,000,009,986.
- **Same attack with the large deposit 1 h after the settlement:** the attacker is still paid 4,166,658,342.

ki65_it.rs:80-89 `rebase()` builds exactly this state (everything settled but one raw token, a rebase, the 3 SOL vest not flushed). No test checks a depositor who joins after the rebase and holds through the vest.

This bypasses a rule the design states for wiped lenders: ECONOMICS.md:1422 says "the wiped lenders keep their unreleased lumps", and decision #44 (ECONOMICS.md:3846) says post-wipe SOL is not the next dust depositor's.

Severity is Medium. The loss is lender yield only: the unreleased vest at the last settlement, made of S2/S3 premium, expiry and penalty lumps and rent top-ups. The settlement principal is not at risk. It needs a full-wipe setup (T=0 while positions are open, then SOL settlement of all remaining borrows). The attacker's cost is negligible (1+X raw tokens, losing 2 units, plus at most lump_vest_s of holding), and the same leak happens without any attacker whenever T is left at dust.

Related disclosures are different mechanisms, not this issue:
- R4B-4 (ECON §9.4): an exiting lender forfeits its vest to those who stay.
- KI-65's conversion-order residual (a JIT depositor with a Sybil placed before the roll): it depends on honest holders rounding to 0 post-rebase shares. Here the honest lenders keep about all of S and still lose the vest.

The code does what the reports say. I ran the repo's own reference model (pool_model.py, which the docs call normative for this math) from a copy in the scratchpad, and the impact is real and close to what the reports claim. The pre-settlement dust deposit is often not even needed.

**Mechanism**
- crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:2316 pays out the unreleased vest (vest_bal) only when token_claims() == 0. If claims are above 0, the vest is not paid out: the branch at 2323-2334 either rebases or does nothing, and vest_bal stays.
- release_in (pool.rs:857-891) later pays that vest to whoever holds shares at release time.
- Shares are priced on tokens only (shares_for_tokens, pool.rs:1668): mint = D·(S+VS)/(T+ΣB_Q+VA). After a rebase, S+VS ≤ R_MAX·(C+VA), where C is the token claims left.
- So a depositor of D raw units ends up with at least D/(D+C+VA) of the shares. With C=1: D=1,000 gives ≥99.8%, and D=10^6 gives ≥99.9998%.
- Nothing blocks that deposit. deposit_in (pool.rs:1923) gates only on a live full-wipe record, and deposit.rs:104-144 checks only amount>0, the mint guard and min_shares. There is no pause or venue check.

**Measured in the reference model** (one 50 SOL settlement with a 3 SOL lump, then a 1 SOL trader sweep, everything claimed after vest_end):
- **Baseline, true wipe (T=0):** the lender gets 50,999,999,999 lamports. The vest is paid out and the sweep goes to the wipe record.
- **Attack, 1 raw unit deposited before the settlement:** the epoch rebases (1/10^9) instead of wiping.
  - A post-settlement deposit of 1,000 raw units takes 3,992,024,811 lamports; the lender drops to 47,007,975,187.
  - With D=10^6 the attacker takes 3,999,992,008 lamports.
  - If the deposit waits 1h or 3h, the attacker takes 3.49 or 2.50 SOL, because the release is linear to the old holders until then.
- **Organic case, no pre-deposit:** in 300 random pools of 2-5 lenders where every lender withdrew all it could while 90% was borrowed, T ended at 1, never 0 (allowance floor, pool.rs:1736).
  - The last settlement therefore always rebases and the vest is never paid out.
  - A depositor of 10^6 raw units right after the settlement took 3,999,992,005 of the 4 SOL. It got back 999,998 of its 10^6 tokens, so the whole cost is 2 raw units, fees and a 6h hold.
  - The honest lenders fell from 50,999,999,997 to 47,000,007,992 lamports.

**Who loses and how much**
- The lenders of a wiped or nearly wiped market lose:
  - all of the vest unreleased at the depositor's entry: S2/S3 take above Q·P_ema, penalty halves, expiry fees, rent top-ups;
  - plus every sweep or cashback until vest_end.
- ECON §9.4's own table (Q worth 500 SOL) puts the S2/S3 premium alone at 27.85-112 SOL.
- The immediate principal is not affected.
- The capture needs no capital at risk. That breaks the stated reason vesting is fair: "a whale must hold its shares through the window, exposed like any lender" (ECON.md:1332).

**Design intent**
- ECON.md:1422 says outright that "the wiped lenders keep their unreleased lumps".
- R4A-7 (ECON.md:1438) treated a 2-raw-unit post-wipe depositor capturing pre-wipe cashback as a finding and fixed it. This is the same class of capture.

**Not disclosed**
- KI-09 / R4B-4 (ECON.md:1356) covers lenders who choose to exit and leave dust behind. Here the lenders still hold their shares.
- KI-65's residual is a JIT depositor taking the vest only after honest holders' shares convert to 0. Here the honest holder keeps about 9×10^5 post-rebase shares.

**Mitigating factors (why Medium, not High)**
- It needs a market where nearly all lent tokens are SOL-settled while free tokens are at dust level (a run before S1/S2/S3).
- The take is limited to the vest window.

**Notes on the fixes**
- The rebase is incidental. Dilution works even when no roll happens, as long as claims are tiny. So "flush on rebase" (Option C) is not complete.
- Flushing at the settlement may let a whale who deposits just before it collect its share of the flushed vest immediately (the JIT snipe R4B-6 removed). That needs a check.

title: On an empty non-wipe market, deposit-sweep-withdraw lets one lender take swept SOL owed to the protocol
root_cause: deposit_in enforces the sweep gate only when total_shares == 0 && is_wipe_live(). On an S = 0 market with no live wipe, a dust deposit lands before sweep_trader. vest_in then vests the swept SOL to the new shares, although with S = 0 it would credit protocol_fees (KI-10). withdraw_in's last-lender flush (shares == total_shares) pays the whole unreleased vest to that same lender in one transaction.
primary_location: crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1939 (deposit_in gate; payout at pool.rs:1831-1837, sweep bit at pool.rs:2118)

members.title: A dust deposit into an empty market takes the trader cashback
A one-transaction lender takes swept SOL that belongs to protocol_fees

verdicts.reason:
The issue holds at commit 55b3e23. Any caller can run the whole path in one transaction, and nothing in the code blocks it.

1. **Deposit gate.** `deposit_in` (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1939) checks the sweep bits only when `total_shares == 0 && is_wipe_live()`. Take a market whose last lender left through ordinary withdrawals: S = 0, `wipe_live` = 0, and the program's `LastSharesBorrowed` check (withdraw.rs:206) forces ΣB_Q = 0. On that market a dust deposit mints shares with no gate. The deposit handler (programs/shortwin/src/instructions/deposit.rs) adds only the amount, `min_shares` and mint-guard checks. With T = 0, VS = 1000 and VA = 1, `a` tokens mint 1000·a shares, and withdrawing them returns exactly `a`, so the attacker loses nothing to rounding.

2. **Sweep.** `sweep_trader` can be called by anyone. Its handler (sweep_trader.rs) asks for the wipe record only while a wipe is live. `pool::sweep` sets no bit (pool.rs:2118, same gate). It then calls `vest_in` (pool.rs:907-950). Because S > 0 now, the SOL goes into `vest_bal` instead of the `credit_in` path that sends it to `protocol_fees` (pool.rs:1014-1025, R3A-10 / KI-10).

3. **Withdraw.** `withdraw` has no cooldown (withdraw.rs docs: "no cooldown (ADOPTED Q22)"). In the same second `release_in` releases 0. The attacker's shares are all of S, so `shares == total_shares && vest_bal != 0` (pool.rs:1831-1837) credits the whole vest to them (realised) and touches again. The handler's built-in `pool::claim` (withdraw.rs:212) then pays it out. The allowance is not a limit here: with ΣB_Q = 0 and no locks it is all of T. The `LenderPosition` rent comes back when the position closes (`closable`).

**Where the SOL comes from.** Value can sit unswept at S = 0. Pump and PumpSwap cashback builds up in the trader's UVA or its pAMM WSOL ATA, and anyone can claim it into the trader PDA with `claim_cashback`. The keeper claims it at most weekly, once it reaches 0.01 SOL (services/keeper/src/sweep.rs duty 13; keeper.example.toml `cashback_interval_s = 604800`, `cashback_min_lamports = 10000000`). So up to a week of cashback earned while lenders were present can still be unclaimed when the market empties. A donation to the trader side can also be taken, but only inside the keeper's 60 s sweep window.

The attack transaction is: deposit(dust), then `claim_cashback(user = trader)`, then `sweep_trader`, then withdraw(all). It moves SOL that, under R3A-10 / KI-10, would go to `protocol_fees`. This is the same dust-depositor capture that R3A-10 was meant to close, reached by putting the deposit first. The R3A-10 regression test (tests/litesvm/tests/lender_it/adversarial.rs:316) and `pool_model.zero_share_demo` only cover sweep-then-deposit. The post-wipe case got exactly this deposit-first gate (R4A-7). The non-wipe S = 0 case did not.

**Severity: Low.** Only the protocol's windfall share is lost. Lenders and borrowers lose nothing, since every lender has already left and the last lender got its vest through the flush. The amount is bounded by the unclaimed venue cashback (at most about one week of the trader's cashback on a cashback coin) plus any third-party donations. No principal is at risk.
verdicts.already_known: Not disclosed. KI-10 (docs/audit/known-issues.md:56) states the rule: SOL that arrives while a market has no lender goes to the protocol. R3A-10 (ARCH:2485, ECON §9.5) marks the dust-depositor capture as FIXED. Neither mentions that putting the deposit before the sweep gets around the rule on a non-wipe S = 0 market. The deposit-first gate exists only for the live-wipe case (R4A-7). The related KI-09 and R4B-4 cover forfeiting the vest when S > 0, not this.

verdicts.reason:
The code confirms the path; I found nothing that blocks it. The real impact is much smaller than "SOL owed to the protocol" sounds.

How it works in one transaction:
1. On a market with S = 0 and no live wipe, deposit_in checks the sweep gate only when `p.total_shares == 0 && p.is_wipe_live()` (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1939). A deposit of a few raw units goes through.
2. With S > 0, sweep_trader books the SOL through vest_in (pool.rs:907-949): vest_bal = X, vest_end = now + lump_vest_s. It never reaches credit_in's protocol branch (pool.rs:1018-1027).
3. withdraw of all shares: release_in releases 0 at the same `now`. Then `shares == p.total_shares && p.vest_bal != 0` (pool.rs:1831-1837) credits all of vest_bal to the attacker's shares. The withdraw instruction pays it in the same call (withdraw.rs, the SOL part of `pool::claim`).
4. LastSharesBorrowed does not stop it. S = 0 without a wipe implies ΣB_Q = 0, because M1-SEC-3 refuses the exit that would leave S = 0 while tokens are borrowed. No position can open inside the attacker's bundle.
5. Pump's `claim_cashback(user = trader)` needs no signature (T-CASHBACK, sweep_trader.rs docs), so outstanding venue cashback can be bundled in front of the sweep.

This goes against the design's stated intent. ECON §9.5 R3A-10 (ECONOMICS.md:1431) says the v0.4 fix leaves "dust depositor claims 0". ARCH:2032 says a JIT deposit around a sweep_trader gets "0 at h = 0". The only test, r3a_10_sol_without_lenders_goes_to_the_protocol (tests/litesvm/tests/lender_it/adversarial.rs:316), runs sweep first and deposit second. The design found this same ordering gap for full wipes (R4A-7, ECON §9.5) and gated only that case.

What can be taken (X):
- Only SOL that reaches the trader side while S = 0. Trading legs move the trader PDAs into market_vault after every leg. No position can exist at S = 0, so no penalties or expiries can arrive.
- So X is the venue cashback still unclaimed when the last lender left, plus donations.
- Cashback exists only on legacy cashback coins, at about 30 bps of the trader's swap volume (docs/research/graduated-venues.md:879).
- The keeper claims it weekly once it reaches 0.01 SOL (services/keeper/keeper.example.toml:222-223). So X is at most about one week of 30 bps of the market's short open/close volume, or under 0.01 SOL. Example: 100 SOL of weekly volume gives about 0.3 SOL.
- X stops growing once S = 0, since no trades can run.
- Attacker cost is close to zero. The deposit comes back, less 1-2 raw units of rounding. On PumpSwap the ATA rent the attacker pays is swept into the vest and flushed back to it.

Who loses:
- Only protocol_fees (fee_recipient), and only the X that a keeper sweep during the S = 0 window would have sent there.
- Former lenders already gave it up under KI-09/KI-10. No current lender exists, so no lender loses.
- Even without an attacker, the protocol's claim is not enforced: an honest first depositor who deposits before any sweep collects X over 6 h.

So this is a small, occasional loss of protocol revenue on cashback coins whose lenders have all left, about the size of R3A-10's original LOW finding. Fair severity: Low.

title: S2/S3 settlement credits Q·P_ema immediately at a frozen pre-halt price to whoever holds shares
root_cause: sol_settle calls waterfall::settle(pos.v, kind, k_s, fv, pos.q, inp.p_ema, inp.r_due), which credits ⌊Q·P_ema/WAD⌋ + R_due to the pool at once. On a halted venue P_ema is the stale pre-halt price, and deposits stay open during the S3 chain. An attacker deposits cheap tokens just before the S3 settlement and takes a pro-rata share of the other lenders' SOL.

members.title: A deposit before an S3 settlement buys SOL at an old P_ema

verdicts.reason:
I could not refute it. The path is real and nothing in the code blocks it.

1. The price is frozen. On a venue that cannot execute, `arming::inputs` takes `p_ema: obs.ema.price` (engine/arming.rs:225). No observation is recorded, so that price is the pre-halt EMA. `spot_leg` returns true when the venue cannot execute (shortwin-math risk.rs:248). `box_of` shrinks the box to the bare EMA point once `!executable && age > RING_LEN` (8 s) (settle.rs:80-84). The `amount_ok` corner check therefore compares P_ema with itself and cannot refuse a stale price. `s3_due` needs only `no_route_now`, the chain and `s3_wait_s`, and expired positions qualify (settle.rs:325-342, 620-626).

2. The immediate credit is valued at that price. sol_settle.rs:257 calls `waterfall::settle(..., pos.q, inp.p_ema, inp.r_due)`. Of the take, `min(x, ⌊Q·P_ema/WAD⌋ + R_due)` is immediate (waterfall.rs:337-374). `pool::settle` -> `true_up` credits `principal − top − credited` (about Q·P_ema) to `acc` and `acc_r` at once (pool.rs:2189-2207, 2273-2296). Every share holding at that moment receives it.

3. Deposits stay open during the S3 chain. `deposit` checks only `amount > 0`, the mint guard, the wipe gate and `min_shares` (deposit.rs:99-157; pool.rs `deposit_in`). It has no venue, halt or `no_route_since` check, and AUDIT.md lists `None` markets as "deposits and withdrawals only". Shares are minted on token units (T + ΣB_Q). `sol_settle` is permissionless and the S3 timer is public. `claim_sol` pays straight from `acc`/`acc_r` with no lock, so the SOL can be taken out in the same transaction. Tokens come back through `withdraw`, which is limited only by `allowance` (by_free ≈ s·T/S). That is effectively the whole claim when the settled position was the last one open.

The bundle [deposit d, sol_settle, claim_sol, withdraw] swaps the attacker's Q·d/(T+B+d) tokens for SOL at P_ema. Against a token price P_true, the attacker gains d/(T+B+d)·Q·(P_ema − P_true), and the other lenders lose exactly that amount. At 9× the pool this is about 90% of the gap. This breaks the stated intent: SPEC line 90 says settlement proceeds above the market value of the debt vest so that a just-in-time deposit gets none of them, and ECON §9.4 R4B-6 says the same. R4B-6 treats ⌊Q·P_ema⌋ as "market value", which only holds while the EMA is live.

Why the severity is Low:
- Several conditions must hold together. The venue must be unable to execute (an admin halt, buys disabled, a graduation elsewhere or a stuck migration). A position must reach S3 while it is liquidatable on the frozen ring or past its deadline. The token must also be cheaper than the frozen P_ema somewhere else. On a stuck migration P_true ≈ P_ema and there is no outside market.
- The loss is limited to the windfall Q·(P_ema − P_true). Existing lenders still receive at least the market value of what they lent, because the attacker only dilutes the upside of the frozen mark.
- On an executable venue (route-broken flag, fee above the cap) the box still applies, and KI-06 bounds that case at fv_dev_bps.
- The project rated the closely related R4B-6 JIT premium capture LOW. One aggravating factor: under KI-24 lenders carry the full downside of the frozen mark (−46% on a 2× move), while this path lets outsiders take most of the upside. That is why someone could argue for Medium.

Related but not the same: KI-24 and KI-43 disclose S3 at the frozen pre-halt P_ema and the lenders' exposure to it. Neither mentions a just-in-time deposit capturing the frozen-price windfall.

The path works as described. The report overstates the impact, though: the attacker swaps its own tokens for SOL at the stale price, so it does not take the other lenders' SOL for free.

What the code shows:
1. Settlement uses the frozen price. sol_settle.rs:257 calls waterfall::settle with inp.p_ema, and arming.rs:225 sets p_ema to obs.ema.price, the stored EMA. A venue that cannot execute records no observation (sol_settle.rs:25-26; ECON §10.3 "Halted venues"), so P_ema stays at its pre-halt value. Up to ⌊q·P_ema/WAD⌋+R_due is paid out immediately (waterfall.rs:351, 368). In pool::settle (pool.rs:2273-2298, true_up at 2189-2205) that principal is credited at once to the shares that exist at that moment.
2. New shares are priced at token par. shares_for_tokens (pool.rs:1668) counts the borrowed q one-for-one with free tokens. Deposits stay open on halted venues: deposit.rs:24 says only mint_unsafe blocks them.
3. The bundle can be atomic. sol_settle is permissionless and the S3 time is public: max(deadline, chain start+s3_wait_s), ECON §10.3. When the settled position is the last open one, resolve_in clears every lock, so [deposit, sol_settle, withdraw, claim_sol] can run in one transaction.

What the attacker actually gains:
- Holding fraction f=d/(C+d) of the shares, the attacker gives up f·q tokens of claim and receives f·⌊q·P_ema⌋ SOL. The rent part goes back to the honest lenders through the pot, and the expiry fee and premium vest over 6 h.
- Net gain is f·q·(P_ema−P_true). It is zero when P_ema matches the market. That is exactly why R4B-6 judged the immediate part safe (ECON §9.4 at line 1334, ARCH 2465; lender_real_it.rs:549-553 says the whale is paid "for the tokens it gave up").
- The honest lenders lose the same amount, but only out of a windfall. Their value is still C·P_true + (1−f)·q·(P_ema−P_true), which never falls below the market value of their claims. The windfall itself is the borrower's overpayment at the frozen price; ECON line 3433 calls a post-dump frozen S3 "lender-favourable, at the borrower's cost". The borrower loses the same amount whether or not the attacker acts.

Example sizes, assuming a 50% dump on other venues and a whale at 9x the pool (f=0.9):
- ECON's frozen RA row (q worth 18.47 SOL at the frozen P_ema): the attacker takes ≈8.3 SOL of the honest lenders' ≈9.2 SOL windfall.
- ECON's 500 SOL settlement example: up to ≈225 SOL.

The real harm is adverse selection. KI-24 has lenders accept −46% when the token pumps 2x during a halt. Outsiders can now join only in the dump case and take almost all of the matching upside, which makes the frozen-mark bet negative for lenders.

Why Low and not higher, all of these must hold together:
- the venue is halted, the market is list-only, or a migration is stuck;
- no pool switch carries the positions;
- the token trades elsewhere below the frozen P_ema;
- the attacker holds or buys tokens worth up to several times the pool.
No principal is lost compared with the market value of the claims.

Not disclosed as such. KI-24 (the frozen pre-halt P_ema mark) and R4B-6 (the immediate part assumed equal to market value) are related, but neither covers outsiders capturing the windfall at a stale P_ema. A possible fix is to vest, or cap, the immediate S3 part when the venue is not executable.

title: Liquidation risk view prices at the live fee tier, which a same-transaction sale or burn raises
root_cause: liquidate::assess (and keeper_exit, sol_settle, engine bounds::reference) quote the risk view at min(φ_live, pos.venue_fee_hard_cap_bps), using read_state_boxed's live fee. On the pump venues φ_live depends on spot market cap/supply. A keeper who sells or burns tokens earlier in the transaction raises the fee tier of the spot and EMA risk quotes and liquidates a healthy position. The fee is not resolved at P_ema (cap_fee_ppm), as it is for opens.

members.title: The liquidation risk view uses a live fee that a sale raises

verdicts.reason:
The path is real and reachable, but only on PumpSwap markets, and the effect is limited to one fee tier.

Path: liquidate.rs:176 calls keeper_exit (ExitKind::Liquidation). keeper_exit reads venues::read_state_boxed(..., venues::mint_supply(&accs.mint)) at liquidate.rs:549-555. That goes through read_state_with to read_state_ema with ema_fee=false (venues/mod.rs:803-816, 842-851). On PumpSwap, pump_amm::read_state builds PammFeeSchedule{base_supply: live supply} and sets fee = fees::pump_amm(effective_quote, base, sch), so the tier is chosen at mcap = effective_quote·supply/base (pump_amm.rs:704-715). fee_ppm_at_ema stays u32::MAX unless ema_fee is set, so cap_fee_ppm() falls back to φ_live (mod.rs:614-625, whose doc says so). assess (liquidate.rs:333-361) prices b_live_risk, the spot leg b_rs, and the EMA leg's quote_at on the ring's cached (x,y) all with state.quoter().capped(pos.venue_fee_hard_cap_bps). The same live fee feeds bounds::reference (bounds.rs:93-95) and sol_settle's risk_quoter (sol_settle.rs:194-206).

Nothing blocks it:
- The cap is 500 bps by default (params.rs:221; ARCH range 300-2,000). PumpSwap's highest tier is 125 bps, so the cap never binds.
- Exits run no open guards or instruction introspection (guard.rs:1-5).
- mint_guard on the exit path checks only the key and owner.
- A holder's SPL burn earlier in the same transaction lowers mint.supply, and liquidate reads the post-burn value. The burn does not touch reserves, so the price, the observation and the ring are unchanged while the tier rises.
- A sale also raises the tier. However, robust_spot = min(p_live, last.lo) (observe.rs:796-797), so the price drop lowers the spot-leg cost and partly offsets the higher fee.

Why the impact is small:
- One tier step on the live FeeConfig is 2-5 bps one-way (graduated-venues.md:294-305). That moves B̂ by at most about 0.05%.
- Crossing a second tier needs the market cap to fall 5% to 120%, because thresholds are thousands of SOL apart. A burn costs about (M − T) SOL of tokens. A sale large enough to cross two tiers lowers the spot leg by more than the fee adds.
- So only positions whose CR is already within about 0.05% of cr_liq_bps on both legs (including all liq_persist_n=3 ring entries) can be flipped, and only while the market cap sits just above a tier threshold. Such a position would be liquidated by any ordinary price tick.
- After a burn the higher fee is permanent. It is the real execution cost, which the SPEC's CR definition uses ("SOL cost to buy back Q now", SPEC.md:110).
- The keeper earns 30% of a 5-10% penalty plus a floor capped at 0.25 SOL, so a burn pays off only in narrow cases.

Other venues:
- Pump curve: not reachable today. short.win picks the curve tier at a fixed 10^15 supply, and pump's curve FeeConfig has a single tier.
- Raydium: fixed fees, not affected.

The extra loosening of B̂_ref/max_in (at most about 5 bps) is negligible next to KI-01's 2% bound.
verdicts.already_known: Partly. The design states that risk quotes and quotes on hypothetical states use the live fee tier: ARCH §4.3 "Two fee views" (ARCHITECTURE.md:1402, 1448), I16 (ARCHITECTURE.md:2099), and ECONOMICS.md row 56 / R3B-7(b) (ECONOMICS.md:104, 314). M7-SEC-5 (ECON #108, ARCH changelog 60, VenueState::cap_fee_ppm doc at venues/mod.rs:599-613) fixes the same same-transaction tier raise for opens only. No known issue in docs/audit/known-issues.md or docs/AUDIT.md covers a keeper raising the tier with a sale or burn before liquidate, expire or sol_settle.

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real. The claimed impact ("liquidates a healthy position") is much larger than what the code and the live fee schedule allow.

Why the path exists:
- liquidate.rs:549-555 reads the venue with `read_state_boxed` and the live `mint_supply`. That goes to `read_state_ema(.., ema_fee=false)` (venues/mod.rs:842-851).
- On PumpSwap, the fee is resolved at mcap = effective_quote·live_supply/base (pump_amm.rs:702-713; fees.rs:199-226). `fee_ppm_at_ema` stays u32::MAX (pump_amm.rs:716-731), so `cap_fee_ppm` is just φ_live on exits.
- `assess` caps only at `pos.venue_fee_hard_cap_bps` (liquidate.rs:333; default 500 bps, above every pump tier). That fee prices `b_live_risk` (338), the spot leg `b_rs` (345, 356) and the EMA leg's ring re-quotes (346-347, 359-364). bounds.rs:94 (`B̂_ref`) and sol_settle.rs:194-205 work the same way.
- Nothing guards against supply or tier changes inside a transaction.
- A burn lowers mcap without moving price. A sale also works if P_live stays at or above lb_lo, because p_rs = min(P_live, lb_lo) (355). Either one raises the risk fee for the spot leg and all `liq_persist_n` (3) ring legs at once, so both legs can flip together.

Why the impact is small:
- Only PumpSwap is exposed. The curve has a single tier (research/pumpfun-bonding-curve.md:151) and fixed 10^15 supply (fees.rs:160). Raydium fees are static.
- The live schedule (research/graduated-venues.md:294-304) steps 5 bps per tier, and only 2-3 bps above 54k SOL. Tiers are thousands of SOL apart, so in practice only the next tier down is reachable. Crossing several tiers needs about a 10-50% mcap drop: a sale that large pushes P_live below lb_lo and lowers B̂_rs, and a burn that large costs that share of the market cap.
- So one step raises every risk quote by about Δφ/(1+φ) ≈ 0.05%. Only positions whose CR on the spot leg and all 3 ring legs is in [L, L·1.0005) can be flipped. For Tier C that is CR 150.00-150.07%.
- The largest jump is 25→95 bps (+70 bps, about 0.7% of B̂). It exists only at the 420-SOL boundary, and only on pools with a default coin creator or a per-pool creator override (fees.rs:215-221). There a short near liquidation has usually risen far above 420 SOL already.
- What the attack needs: mcap just above a tier threshold, plus a position already within about one fee step of L. The cost is either a burn of δ·mcap worth of tokens, or a sale round trip with room above lb_lo.

Who loses and how much:
- The borrower pays the penalty (5-10% of min(B̂_live_risk, B̂_ref), SPEC §4; about 5% of V for Tier C). The keeper takes 30% plus the floor.
- The venue also charges about 5 bps more on the buyback; that goes to pump and the creator, not the attacker.
- These positions sit about 5 bps of price from liquidation, so an honest per-second keeper would almost always liquidate them moments later anyway. What is actually taken is an earlier liquidation and the borrower's small chance of recovering, not a liquidation of a truly healthy position.
- In sol_settle, S1 at the gap line leaves the borrower at most about Δφ·B̂.
- No lender loss.

Docs:
- V2-1 (ARCH:1448, ECON:314) and R3B-7 b (ARCH:1402) set exit risk quotes at the live tier.
- The M7-SEC-5 fix covers open_short only, by choice ("no other instruction pays it", ARCH:1601; ECON #108).
