- FITS-2 (ECON:512, 1101, N29) shows the design intends that nothing done inside the same transaction can make the spot leg true. This fee lever is not covered there, and it is not listed in docs/audit/known-issues.md.

title: withdraw_in resets b_min only when lock_norm == 0, so locks set at a higher ΣB_Q keep a stale low b_min
root_cause: withdraw_in sets v.b_min = p.borrowed_q only if v.lock_norm == 0, and lock_norm is tested before the lender's own live term leaves the calendar. Another live lock, the lender's own lock, or a rebase residue keeps lock_norm > 0, so a new lock taken at a higher ΣB_Q inherits the old low b_min. resolve_in decays Π only when bn < b_min, so those locks never decay.

members.title: Later locks never decay while an earlier lock holds a low b_min

verdicts.reason:
The mechanics are real and any lender can reach them. But this is the specified single-index design, not a coding slip, and its effect is limited to over-locking that ends at lock_until.

Code path:
- programs/shortwin/src/instructions/withdraw.rs:194 calls pool::withdraw. No other handler writes b_min (grep finds only the vault.rs load/store at 74/88).
- In withdraw_in (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1806-1808), b_min = ΣB_Q happens only when new_lock != 0 && lock_norm == 0. The test reads lock_norm after touch_in's cal_advance (pool.rs:1633) and before the lender's own live term is removed (cal_sub, pool.rs:1809-1811).
- resolve_in (pool.rs:1898-1901) decays Π only when lock_norm > 0 && bn < b_min.
- So while any term sits in the calendar, b_min stays at the running minimum of ΣB_Q since lock_norm last hit 0. A lock taken later at a higher ΣB_Q gets no decay while ΣB_Q falls back toward that minimum. Below it, the lock decays only by B'/b_min_old, not by B'/B_at_lock.

All three sub-paths hold:
1. Another lender's live lock keeps lock_norm > 0.
2. The withdrawer's own live term keeps it > 0, because the test runs before cal_sub.
3. Rebase residue: rollover floors each bucket as a whole (pool.rs:2354-2358) and each l.lock_term separately (pool.rs:1231). Σ⌊term_i·num/den⌋ ≤ ⌊Σterm_i·num/den⌋, so a remainder is left in the bucket. Also, a lender whose l.lock floors to 0 never runs cal_sub (cur == 0), so its whole scaled term stays in the bucket until its day ends.

Nothing in code blocks any of this. The Rust matches the reference model line for line (docs/design/sim/pool_model.py:638-641 and 546-548).

Why the severity is Low:
- No funds are created or stolen. b_min never ends up above ΣB_Q while lock_norm > 0, so there is no wrong over-decay.
- The only harm is that later lockers stay locked too long. Their allowance stays lower than fair, and returned T goes pro-rata to unlocked shares (allowance = u·T/(S−locked), pool.rs:1730-1738). An unlocked co-lender can therefore leave first and push more of a later SOL-settlement loss onto the over-locked lender.
- Example: two equal lenders, ΣB_Q 100 → 1800 → 200 with a 50% settlement. About 33 of a 100-token loss moves to the over-locked lender, and it cannot withdraw until lock_until.
- Every lock still ends at lock_until (lock_of, pool.rs:1697; calendar expiry). lock_until is at most about 101 days and typically about 31.
- An attacker keeping a dust lock alive gains little. In a busy market overlapping locks keep b_min stale anyway.

Possible fixes, if wanted: a per-lock or per-cohort decay base, re-basing b_min when a lock is set above it, or resetting b_min from a live-lock count rather than lock_norm.
verdicts.already_known:
Partly. The rule itself is documented as intended:
- ECON §9.3 (docs/design/ECONOMICS.md:1248): 'elif locks exist and B' < b_min … (net reductions only, V2-3)'.
- ARCH A57 (docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:2326): 'Π decays only when ΣB_Q falls below its running minimum since the first lock of the Π epoch'.
- ARCH §3.3 lock update (ARCHITECTURE.md:1062): 'if new_lock > 0 ∧ lock_norm == 0, b_min = ΣB_Q'.
- The 'growing, always busy' table in ECON §9.3 (ECONOMICS.md:1275-1277) shows Π returns 0% there and only lock_until (R3B-1) frees the lender.

Not covered: AUDIT.md has no known-issue entry for the specific consequence. Nothing names cross-lender inheritance of a stale low b_min by locks set at a higher ΣB_Q, the own-term ordering, or rebase-residue terms keeping lock_norm > 0 after no live lock remains.

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real, but it is the specified design. The impact is overstated: locks do decay later, and they always expire.

What the code does:
- pool.rs:1806-1808 sets `b_min = ΣB_Q` only when `lock_norm == 0`, and it runs before the lender's own term leaves the calendar at :1809-1812.
- resolve_in (pool.rs:1899-1901) scales Π only when `bn < b_min`.
- So a lock taken at a higher ΣB_Q keeps the earlier, lower b_min.

I ran pool_model.py v0.4.1 in a scratchpad copy (scratchpad/bmin_sim/sim.py). Setup: lenders A, C, D hold 10/45/45% of 1e12; 100e9 is borrowed and A takes its allowance (b_min = 100e9); borrowing rises to 800e9; C takes its allowance; then 700e9 is repaid.
- **Stale b_min:** Π stays at WAD. All 395e9 of C's remaining value stays locked, C's allowance is 0 and D's is its full 450e9.
- **Counterfactual (C's lock is the first one):** Π falls to 0.125 WAD, C's allowance is 295e9 and D's is 421e9.

Why "never decay" is wrong:
- Π still decays, by B'/b_min, once ΣB_Q falls below the old b_min.
- At ΣB_Q = 0 the epoch rolls and every lock clears (pool.rs:1891-1896).
- Every lock expires at `lock_until` whatever Π does: lock_of returns 0 at pool.rs:1697, and cal_advance drops the bucket at :745-771.
- `lock_until` = day end of max(now, max_release) + lock_grace_s. With the default tiers (tier.rs:94, 30 d) and grace (params.rs:213, 1 d) that is about 31 d (sim: 30.96 d). The compiled maximum is about 101 d.
- The rebase residue (floored bucket scaling, pool.rs:2354) sits in the same day bucket as the lock it came from, so it expires on the same day.

Impact:
- Withdrawals are delayed for a lender who locks later, bounded by `lock_until`. Over-locking is the conservative direction: I-P4 (allowances ≤ T) still holds and no tokens or SOL are taken.
- The only value effect is conditional. If the remaining borrowed inventory is later settled at a loss, unlocked lenders such as D can exit ahead of C. That is the run residual already disclosed as KI-13 (bounded at +4.3% to +11.1%). In the example D escapes about 29e9 more exposure than it otherwise could.

It is intended:
- ARCH A57 (ARCHITECTURE.md:2326) and ECON §9.3 (ECONOMICS.md:1248) define b_min as the running minimum "since the first lock of the Π epoch" and make lock_until the bound when borrowing does not fall ("Why lock_until (R3B-1)").
- The vector `scripted_overlock` (gen_pool.py:1296-1328) pins "B_Q back to b_min: no decay (V2-3)".

The report's Option B fix would reopen V2-3:
- A runner locks at a low ΣB_Q, then makes a dust re-lock at a higher ΣB_Q to re-base b_min. When borrowing falls back, its old lock decays by B_low/B_high.
- That would break the "churn never reduces a lock" property (lender_it/adversarial.rs:339-380; hook M1-FID-9 in tests/litesvm/src/invariants/lender.rs:1009).
- Testing `lock_norm` before the own term leaves the calendar is what blocks this re-basing by the lender itself.

The only real gap is in the docs: ECON's figure of "94% within 24 h when interest fades" holds only for the lender that set b_min, not for lenders who lock later.
verdicts.already_known: Intended design rather than a register row. ARCHITECTURE.md:2326 (A57: "Π decays only when ΣB_Q falls below its running minimum since the first lock of the Π epoch"). ARCHITECTURE.md:2579 (V2-3). ECONOMICS.md:1248 and the §9.3 paragraph "Why lock_until (R3B-1)" (locks that do not decay under Π are bounded only by lock_until). Vector gen_pool.py:1296-1328 `scripted_overlock` ("B_Q back to b_min: no decay (V2-3)"). The value side is KI-13, the run residual (docs/audit/known-issues.md:59). The specific case of later locks inheriting the first lock's b_min is not listed as its own row in docs/audit/known-issues.md.

title: A new lock era resets b_min but not Π, so Π compounds across eras down to 1
root_cause: When lock_norm reaches 0 and a new lock starts, withdraw_in resets b_min but keeps v.pi. Π resets only when resolve_in sees q ≥ ΣB_Q, i.e. a full repay. Repeated partial borrow/repay eras multiply Π by bn/b_min (Ceil) each time until Π reaches 1 wei. lock_of = ⌈lock·Π/lock_pi⌉ then never shrinks, so later locks never decay.

members.title: Repeated lock eras drive Π to 1, so later locks never decay

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real, and a permissionless actor can reach it.

**Code path**
- `withdraw_in` (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs:1806-1808) sets `v.b_min = p.borrowed_q` whenever a new lock starts while `lock_norm == 0`. It never touches `v.pi` or `v.pi_epoch`.
- `resolve_in` (pool.rs:1888-1904) puts Π back to WAD only when `q >= p.borrowed_q` (1890-1896). Otherwise it sets `Π = ceil(Π·bn/b_min)` (1900).
- Nothing else resets Π:
  - the calendar drain `cal_advance` (745-771) only empties buckets;
  - the share-epoch roll (2351-2358) scales buckets and can even floor `lock_norm` to 0, but leaves Π alone;
  - the program only copies the math structs (programs/shortwin/src/state/vault.rs:69-90).
- So every lock era ends when the buckets expire, and the next era multiplies Π by a fresh ratio `B'/b_min`, starting from the higher, re-borrowed b_min. Π compounds across eras instead of telescoping.

**Example trace (ratio 1e-3 per era)**
1. Era 1: ΣB_Q = 1e14 (a big short plus a dust short of 1e11). Any lender withdraws (add>0), so b_min = 1e14. The big short is repaid (`repay` → `close_pos` 2160 → `resolve_in`), so Π = 1e15.
2. The locks pass `lock_until` (`lock_until_for` 849: `max_release` + grace, at least 1 h, default 1 d). `cal_advance` brings `lock_norm` to 0. Π stays at 1e15.
3. Era 2: the big short is reopened (`borrow` 2141). A new lock sets b_min = 1e14 again (1807). The repay takes Π to 1e12.
4. After 6 eras Π = 1. From then on `ceil(1·bn/b_min) = 1` whatever is repaid.
5. `lock_of` (1696-1701) = `ceil(lock·1/1)` = the full lock. Repayments never shrink it; only time-based expiry at `lock_until` releases it.

**Actor and cost**
- One party needs only the permissionless trader and lender roles. It needs:
  - capital to borrow a large part of the inventory each era;
  - one min-notional position kept open the whole time, so ΣB_Q never reaches 0 (default `min_notional` is 1e8 lamports, params.rs:189);
  - several days per era.
- The fee and rent cost is real, and the party gains nothing from it. Organic borrow/repay cycles across quiet spells drift Π the same way, only more slowly.

**Impact (why Low)**
- No funds are lost and I-P4 still holds (locked ≤ Σ lock_i, so unlocked allowances still sum to at most T).
- Π decay is disabled, so a lender who withdrew cannot take back tokens that have returned until `lock_until`. That is up to `max_release` + grace, and `max_release` is a running maximum that can reach about 93 days ahead. This is the 'lock_until alone' baseline that ECON (ECONOMICS.md:108) calls worse but safe.
- The effect lasts until ΣB_Q reaches 0, and that one event clears it completely.
- Secondary effect: with Π tiny, the term `floor(new_lock·WAD/Π)` (1814-1818) can overflow u128. That makes `withdraw` fail with `Overflow`, but only for pools whose shares-per-token ratio has grown toward R_MAX (1e6, line 79).

**Spec match**
The behavior matches `pool_model.py` exactly (lines 534-548 and 638-639). It is a spec-level flaw, not a deviation from the sim.
verdicts.already_known: Partly disclosed. ARCHITECTURE.md §9 M0b carried-over note (1) (docs/design/ARCHITECTURE.md:2189) says 'Π resets only at ΣB_Q = 0' and proposes 'roll the Π epoch whenever lock_norm reaches 0', which is the fix this finding gives. But the note only discusses the single-era overflow, claims 'Π telescopes to ≈ WAD·ΣB_Q/b_min' and calls it unreachable. The b_min reset at pool.rs:1807 without a Π reset breaks that telescoping bound across eras, and the note does not mention the loss of lock decay. The issue is not in docs/audit/known-issues.md or AUDIT.md.

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real, but the impact is smaller than the title says. Locks taken at a tiny Π stop shrinking as loans are repaid, yet they still expire at lock_until.

How it happens (crates/shortwin-math/src/pool.rs):
- At :1806-1808 `withdraw_in` sets `b_min = borrowed_q` whenever `new_lock != 0 && lock_norm == 0`, but does not touch `v.pi`.
- Π returns to WAD only at :1890-1896, when `resolve_in` sees `q >= borrowed_q` (a full repay). Nothing else in the crate or program writes Π (grep: only :411 init, :1892, :1900).
- At :1898-1901 Π becomes ⌈Π·bn/b_min⌉. Inside one era this telescopes to WAD·B_min/B_first. Across eras, b_min restarts at the current ΣB_Q while Π does not, so the per-era ratios multiply.
- `lock_norm` can now reach 0 in the middle of a Π epoch, through calendar expiry (`cal_advance` :745-771), with no repay. The design text (ARCH:1062, "first lock of the Π epoch") still assumes that cannot happen.
- The code matches the reference sim exactly (pool_model.py:534-548, 638-639), so this is a design flaw, not an implementation slip.

Quantified:
- **Attacker path.** The per-market open-notional cap is 25 SOL and min_notional is 0.1 SOL, so one era can cut Π by at most about 250x at a steady price. Π goes 1e18 → 4e15 → 1.6e13 → 6.4e10 → 2.6e8 → 1.0e6 → 4.1e3 → 16 → 1, so 8 eras reach Π = 1.
- **Each era's requirements.** All locks must expire, which takes at least the end of the day after max(now, max_release) + lock_grace_s. ΣB_Q must also stay above 0, by keeping a min-notional position rolling.
- **Attacker cost and gain.** The attacker pays fees and rent on repeated borrows of up to 25 SOL and gains nothing directly. This is griefing.
- **Organic path.** It is much slower: about 53 eras at a ratio of 0.5 per era.
- **Before Π reaches 1.** The ceiling in ⌈Π·bn/b_min⌉ already discards any single repay smaller than B/Π, because b_min still drops while Π stays put. At Π below about 250, closing a minimum-size position no longer shrinks any lock.
- **At Π = 1.** `lock_of` (:1695-1700) gives ⌈lock·1/1⌉ = lock, a constant, until ΣB_Q reaches 0. One live position anywhere keeps it there.
- **Who is affected.** A lender who withdraws while tokens are borrowed has the borrowed part of that withdrawal held until lock_until, instead of having it released as borrowers repay. Per ECON §9.3 that means 0% back for about 31 days instead of 94% within 24 h. The compiled maximum horizon is 90 + 3 + 7 + 1 days.
- **What is not affected.** No principal is lost, and share value is unchanged. The aggregate is floored (`locked_total` :1709-1711, term floor at :1815-1819), so it never exceeds the sum of individual locks and allowances still never sum above T (I-P4 holds). Lenders without a lock are not hurt; their allowance u·T/su gets slightly larger.

Why Low:
- Lenders lose access to part of their funds for a while, nothing is stolen, and the lock_until backstop bounds it.
- The design already accepts the lock_until-only outcome as the worst case for a busy market ("growing, always busy: 0% until day 32", ECONOMICS.md table after :1271). This issue pushes the fading-interest case down to that accepted worst case.
- The overflow side effect (term = ⌊new_lock·WAD/Π⌋) is negligible at Π ≥ 1. Shares are at most about raw·R_MAX = 1e6, so terms stay below u128 for realistic pool sizes.

title: new_raydium seeds L_slow at the 2D anchor instead of capping it at the locked depth D
root_cause: Observation::new_raydium builds the state with Self::new(now, p, l_sample.min(cap)), cap = ⌊D·10⁴/λ_min⌋ (2D at λ_min 50%), so L_slow = L_ema = min(l_sample, 2D). A Raydium adoption (rewrite_liquidity) instead keeps L_slow ≤ D. A deposit wrapped around the price start therefore seeds L_slow at up to twice the locked depth, which ref_liquidity then credits. This compounds with I-14's 2D cap.

members.title: A Raydium price start sets L_slow above the locked depth

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real, and anyone can reach it on the Raydium paths. It does not affect the PumpSwap caller.

Code:
- `crates/shortwin-math/src/observe.rs:398-402`: `new_raydium` calls `Self::new(now, p, l_sample.min(cap))`. `Ema::new` (`observe.rs:136-148`) sets `liq_slow = l`, so `L_slow = min(l_sample, cap)`.
- `cap = depth_at_lambda(D, pool_lock_min_bps)`. The default is 5,000 bps (`params.rs:223`), so cap = 2D. The bounds are [2,000, 10,000] bps (`params.rs:973`), so cap ranges from D to 5D.
- A Raydium adoption takes a different branch. `RaydiumLocked` sets `liq_slow = min(L_slow, D)` (`observe.rs:926-930`).

Reachability:
- **Raydium listing.** `create_market.rs:661-666` calls `initial_raydium` (`engine/observe.rs:82-85`). `create_market` is "anyone lists a mint".
- **First adoption on a list-only market that never had a price.** This is `pool_select.rs:594,608-610`, called from `propose_pool.rs:269`. `propose_pool` has no signer.
- In both paths `l_sample` is the candidate's live sqrt(X*Y), read in that same instruction. A Raydium deposit/withdraw wrapped around it raises the sample. It does not move D, which is deposit-invariant (`bounds.rs:89-91`).
- On a pool with all LP burned (lambda about 100%, honest sqrt(X*Y) = D), one atomic bundle therefore sets L_slow to 2D instead of D.

Nothing caps L_slow later on Raydium:
- `warm_step` keeps `liq_slow` and `slow_ts` (`..*ema`, `observe.rs:690-700`).
- `refresh_locked_depth` caps L_slow at D only on PumpSwap (`prologue.rs:216-218`).
- `steady_step` decays L_slow only with tau = 3,600 s and dts <= 60 s (`observe.rs:624-626`).
- The PumpSwap caller (`pump_amm.rs:883-887`) is not affected. Its lambda_min is `PUMPSWAP_LOCK_MIN_BPS = 10_000` (`consts.rs:77`), so cap = D, and the prologue also caps L_slow at D.

Who reads the inflated L_slow:
- `ref_liquidity` credits it up to the 2D cap (`bounds.rs:100-109`).
- `conservative_x0` computes min(X_now, L_slow/sqrt(P), 2D/sqrt(P)) (`caps.rs:252-268`).
- The tier takes `r_eff = min(R_now, R_slow)` (`tier.rs:267-268`; `engine/tier.rs:56`).
- So the attacker can wrap a second deposit around its own later open. That lifts X_now, and sizing and tier then bind at the inflated L_slow. This breaks the "a deposit wrapped around the open inflates nothing" property that the PumpSwap sim relies on (`pumpswap_lp.out` part 3 (c)). It does so with two atomic deposits, where I-14's 2D bound needs a deposit held in the pool.

Why the severity is Low:
- Opens wait `pool_list_window_s` (default 3,600 s, `open_short.rs:290-296`) plus the warm-up.
- With cranks at most 60 s apart, the excess decays by about 1/e per hour. At the first open L_slow is about 1.37D instead of D; it stays higher if the market is rarely cranked or the window is set lower.
- The effect never exceeds the already disclosed lambda/lambda_min (2D) cap.
- The attacker needs about 1x the pool's reserves in both assets inside one transaction, and must be the one who starts the market's price.
- Harm is conditional: an oversized position against the real depth leads to S1 or lender loss only in a genuine gap. The tighter exit bound is a minor side effect at about 1.37x.

Prior disclosure:
- The owner fixed the analogous PumpSwap residual (L_slow about 1.35x the depth for about an hour) as M6R-1 (`ECONOMICS.md:469`; `pumpswap_lp.out` part 2).
- `ARCHITECTURE.md:2207` says a Raydium price start is "a little" less strict, but only in terms of honest third-party LP.
- The sim does not model a Raydium price start (`shortwin_sim.py:96`).
- The known-issues register has no entry for this.

The code does what the report says, but the impact is smaller than claimed.

The mechanism is real. crates/shortwin-math/src/observe.rs:398-402 calls Self::new(now, p, l_sample.min(cap)), and Ema::new at :136-149 sets liq_slow equal to that value. So a Raydium price start gives L_slow = min(sqrt(X*Y), floor(D*1e4/lambda_min)), which is 2D at the default pool_lock_min_bps of 5,000. An adoption instead keeps L_slow <= D, through rewrite_liquidity RaydiumLocked at observe.rs:926-930 and pool_select.rs:617-620. Two call sites are affected: create_market.rs:665 and pool_select.rs:609 (a list-only market's first adoption; adopted_l_slow at :409-418 mirrors it). Both are permissionless, so one transaction of [deposit >= pool size, create_market or propose_pool, withdraw] reaches the cap. On the lambda 92-99.8% pools the design targets (ARCH line 810), that is about 2x the honest depth. No code clamps it afterwards: the warm-up clamp L_slow = min(L_slow, D) in prologue.rs:211-218 runs only on PumpSwap.

The report overstates the impact in five ways:
(1) The pump_amm.rs:887 call site is not affected. start_price uses cap = depth_at_lambda(D, PUMPSWAP_LOCK_MIN_BPS = 10,000), which equals D (pump_amm.rs:883), and refresh_locked_depth clamps L_slow to D as well.
(2) It does not compound with the 2D reference cap. ref_liquidity takes min(max(L_ema', L_slow), depth_cap) (bounds.rs:106-108), and depth_cap is the same floor(D*1e4/lambda_min). Every other reader on Raydium caps at the same value: conservative_x0's x_lock (caps.rs:261-267) and the tier's lock bound (tier.rs:29-31). The credit never goes above 2D.
(3) Nobody is exposed at the start. A price start has no positions, and right after it L_ema' = L_mlo = the same seeded l, so L_slow adds nothing to the reference. Opens wait for ema_warm == 0 (8 integrations; warm_step leaves L_slow and slow_ts unchanged) and for the listing window. adopt() sets pool_seen_at = now because inside is false when from == None (pool_select.rs:597-605), and create_market also sets it to now. The window defaults to 3,600 s.
(4) The excess decays before the first open. With tau_slow = 3,600 s, slow_dtmax = 60 s and the keeper's 60-s listing cadence, about 52 steady steps follow an 8-minute warm-up, and (3600/3660)^52 is about 0.42. At the open gate L_slow is about 1.42D instead of about 1.0D. Its half-life is about 42 minutes of integrations.
(5) An attacker can get most of this without the bug. After the guard clears at the end of the warm-up, deposit-wrapped cranks in the many seconds the keeper leaves free on a zero-position market feed lobs = min(deposit, 2*L_ema) = 2D into L_slow. bounds.rs:86-89 acknowledges this push. Without the seed, an attacker who owns about 59/60 of the slow weight reaches about 1.57D at the gate; with it, about 2D. The two converge within a few hours.

What can actually go wrong: an atomic [deposit, open_short, withdraw] inflates x_now, so x_slow is the only term binding. A position could then be sized at about 1.4x the honest cap at the default window, or up to 2x if governance sets pool_list_window_s to 0, which its bounds of [0, 86,400] allow. While L_slow still sits above the live depth, a genuine pump can fail the exit bound and push that position to S1. That is the ECON §12.12 (12)(e) mechanism, where a 1.9x position lost lenders 29.3% of Q on PumpSwap.

Who loses: lenders, and only if a genuine pump lands within that decay window. The attacking borrower is zeroed in S1 and takes nothing; the attacker pays only transaction fees and needs flash capital about the pool's size. This is a bounded bypass of a risk limit, not theft. Severity: Low.
verdicts.already_known: Not in the known-issues register (docs/audit/known-issues.md, KI-01 to KI-68). The behaviour is what the spec asks for: ECON §5.2 (ECONOMICS.md line 478, "L_ema = L_slow = min(sqrt(X*Y), cap)"), the ECON table at line 238, ARCH §4.4 line 1521 and ARCH §2.6 line 823. The wider class, crediting up to D/lambda_min on Raydium, was accepted by the owner: SPEC §14 M6D-1 (SPEC.md line 338) says "Raydium keeps sizing on its locked liquidity over the 50 % minimum". bounds.rs:86-97 also discloses that pushes can lift L_slow to the cap once the guard clears. The docs never compare the price start's L_slow with the adoption's L_slow <= D or with PumpSwap's warm-up clamp.

title: Raydium ref_depth_cap credits ⌊D·10⁴/λ_min⌋ (2D), so a held-then-pulled deposit lifts L_b over the live pool
root_cause: engine::bounds::ref_depth_cap passes the venue's λ_min (pool_lock_min_bps, 50%) to shortwin_math::bounds::ref_depth_cap → depth_at_lambda, so ref_liquidity caps its EMA terms at 2D rather than D on Raydium. PumpSwap uses 100% instead. A borrower who holds a deposit into the deadline and pulls it leaves L_ema/L_slow credited up to 2D. The buyback then exceeds the bound, blocking Raydium liquidate and expire for over an hour.

members.title: A pulled deposit blocks Raydium liquidate and expire for over an hour

verdicts.reason:
The mechanism is real and reachable for expiry. The liquidation part of the claim is overstated.

Code path:
- `VenueKind::lock_min_bps` returns `pool_lock_min_bps` for RaydiumV4 and RaydiumCpmm (state/market.rs:149-155). `engine::bounds::ref_depth_cap` (engine/bounds.rs:48-51) passes that value to `shortwin_math::bounds::ref_depth_cap` → `depth_at_lambda` (crates/shortwin-math/src/bounds.rs:166-168). At the default 5,000 bps the cap is 2D.
- `keeper_exit` calls it for both liquidate and expire (instructions/liquidate.rs:571-572). It then reaches `ref_liquidity` (crates/shortwin-math/src/bounds.rs:100-109): `L_b = max(L_live, min(max(L_ema', L_slow), cap))`.
- D = λ·√(XY) (pool_select.rs:41-51). It does not change on a deposit or a withdrawal, so a deposit cannot lower the cap.
- In steady state (no venue switch) `ema.guard = 0`. `steady_step` then feeds the held deposit's real depth straight into `L_slow` with τ_slow = 3,600 s (observe.rs:330, 624-626).
- Raydium deposits and withdrawals are permissionless. The keeper's duty-2 coverage does not help: a held deposit is the pool's real √(XY), not a foreign observation.

- On 0.25% pools (c ≤ 0.75%) the ratio is about 0.4%, so expiry is not held up.
- For positions sized on D, liquidations are not blocked: δ_liq 2% covers the 1.27% (ECON §8.2; (12)(f)(i): 120 of 120 cells give the same exit second).

That happens on λ<1 pools whose unlocked LP leaves; that case does not depend on the cap and is disclosed (ECON §12.12 (5b)(vi)). It also happens when a position is sized while a deposit is held, which is a sizing root cause, not this one.

Impact: the borrower can always close, and lenders are not hurt beyond their tokens staying out for about an hour. Pulling it off ties up 2-3× the pool's capital for an hour, and the payoff is only a delayed expiry. That makes it Low.

- λ_live must be at least about 0.83-0.86, because the cap is (λ_live/λ_min)·L_live. A pool locked at 50 % has no exposure.
- The position must have c > 1.96 %. That requires a fee of at least about 0.66 %, since the fee-scaled cap 3·φ is 0.75 % at 25 bps. - A genuine third-party LP leaving at the deadline triggers the same delay with no attacker at all.

- The borrower gets about 30-60 minutes past the deadline with no expiry fee.
- Rent keeps accruing through the market index (`rent.rs:342`). The extension is not rent-free for the borrower, and the lenders are paid for the time.
- The lenders' tokens stay out past their guaranteed horizon. The docs measured no lender principal loss: if the price pumps, the position becomes a liquidation, and liquidations pass.

- The liquidation bound uses `δ_liq` = 2 % (`liquidate.rs:439-441`).
- At the 2.47 % cap the drained-versus-2D gap is 1.27 %. Blocking would need c_live of about 3.85 % or more.

- The M6E-1 expiry fix was applied to PumpSwap only.
- No known-issue entry and no ECON residual covers the Raydium expiry hold.

**Severity: Low.** The effect is a liveness delay of tens of minutes, which costs heavy capital to cause, and no fund loss.

title: evaluate step 2 refreshes a lapsed arming clock instead of letting it re-arm
root_cause: In settle::evaluate step 2 (not liquidatable, not expired), an armed position that fails not_liquidatable gets state.last = now unconditionally. That includes a clock that has already lapsed (not is_live(now, arm_gap_s)). One sol_settle call in a calm second revives the old arm count, so the next call settles S1/S2 at once.

members.title: Step 2 of evaluate revives a lapsed clock with its old count

verdicts.reason:
The defect is real and nothing in the code blocks it.

**The code path**
- Step 2 (crates/shortwin-math/src/settle.rs:556-566) writes `state.last = now` whenever `state.armed != 0` and `not_liquidatable` is false. It never checks `is_live`.
- Step 3 handles this correctly. It computes `live` (settle.rs:571), refreshes `last` only when the clock is live (settle.rs:610-617), and re-arms a lapsed clock with `count = ema_count` (settle.rs:589-593).
- After a step-2 refresh, the next step-3 call finds `is_live` true (settle.rs:366-368). It does not re-arm, so `updates = ema_count - old_count` (settle.rs:596-600) is already at least `persist_n`, and S1/S2 executes immediately (settle.rs:600-605).
- The old count cannot cause an Underflow revert. `ema_count` only increases (observe.rs:627 and :687), and `mark_restart` (observe.rs:155) does not reset it.
- On-chain: sol_settle.rs:241-245 calls `evaluate`, and sol_settle.rs:367 stores the clock. `set_arm_state` is called only there and at position init (state/position.rs:157), so no other instruction clears a lapsed arm. `sol_settle` is permissionless (AUDIT.md §4 role table).

**How it is reached**
- A clock lapses naturally whenever no step-3 evaluation lands for more than `arm_gap_s`:
  - the venue cannot execute: step 3 is skipped (settle.rs:570) and the keeper only watches (keeper decide.rs:342-350);
  - the warm-up gate is active (settle.rs:546-549; decide.rs:351-352);
  - the keeper is in a Liquidate or LiquidateWait plan (decide.rs:368-397);
  - the keeper is down.
- The honest keeper then makes the reviving step-2 call itself. For an armed, not-liquidatable position it sends SolSettle (decide.rs:357-359).
- An attacker can also force step 2 inside one transaction. The spot leg uses `P_rs = min(P_live, lb_lo)` (observe.rs:796-798) and `l_spot = max(L_live, ...)` (bounds.rs:156-157). A token dump or an LP deposit therefore makes the spot leg false, so `cr_liquidatable` is false and the call enters step 2. The ring-based EMA leg is unaffected, so `not_liquidatable` stays false and the clock is kept. The attacker unwinds, then calls sol_settle again for S1/S2.
- The I12 hook (tests/litesvm/src/invariants/positions.rs:14) only checks that the clock was live in the state just before the call, so it passes this.

**It follows the spec, which is inconsistent**
- ARCH §3.8 step 2 (ARCHITECTURE.md:1218) says "if armed ... otherwise keep the clock (s_last = now)". The normative sim does the same (shortwin_sim.py:1957-1961).
- That contradicts ECON §5.6 (ECONOMICS.md:550), "Evaluations more than settle_arm_gap_s apart re-arm it", and the code's own doc comment at settle.rs:410.

**Why Low**
- It needs an existing arm from a real box-robust S1/S2 event that was neither settled nor disarmed.
- When it executes, the S1/S2 legs must still hold on the box (live, robust spot, corner (P_lo, L_hi)), and `refuted` must be false. The decision still rests on manipulation-resistant evidence.
- What is lost is only the `persist_n` persistence window (40 EMA updates by default, up to 600). The borrower is harmed only if the market would have recovered inside it. On S1 the borrower gets 0; S2 is capped at fair value, so the loss there is small.
- By design, an old count already survives any length of evaluated, non-refuted time (step-2 and step-3 keeps). The bug only adds forgiveness for unobserved gaps longer than `arm_gap_s`.
- While the honest keeper is running, it usually disarms healthy armed positions through step 2, which limits how many stale arms exist.

   - a venue that cannot execute, since step 3 is skipped (settle.rs:570);

Box-robust refutation or "not liquidatable" at the reviving call still disarms (settle.rs:558, 572).

- Lenders are not harmed in expectation: the ECON §5.7 lag study shows that an earlier S1 in a genuine move helps them.

title: Under the post-change guard the spot-leg liquidity floor reads bucket lows that withdraw-wrapped cranks lower
root_cause: bounds::spot_liquidity floors L_live at guarded_ema_liquidity, which while ema.guard != 0 is min(L_ema, ring_liq_lower_median). That median is the lower median of bucket lows (llo), and withdraw-wrapped cranks push it down. An unlocked LP holder drains both L_live and the floor and force-liquidates a healthy position.

members.title: Under the guard, an LP holder forces liquidation at a drained depth

verdicts.reason:
The code works the way the finding says, but the attack only succeeds in a narrow case, and the harm stays inside a bound the owner has already accepted.

How it works:
- **The floor.** `spot_liquidity` returns `max(L_live, guarded_ema_liquidity)` (crates/shortwin-math/src/bounds.rs:156-158). While `ema.guard != 0`, that floor is `min(L_ema, ring_liq_lower_median)` (bounds.rs:117-122).
- **Bucket lows are a minimum.** `record` sets `llo = min` over every observation in the second (observe.rs:448-468). One `[withdraw all, crank_price, deposit]` in a second therefore sets that bucket's `llo = D`, even if the keeper's honest crank lands in the same second. The keeper cannot lift it.
- **Four wrapped seconds are enough.** `ring_liq_lower_median` takes index 3 of the 8 sorted lows (observe.rs:732-749). So 4 wrapped seconds out of 8 give `L_mlo = D`.
- **`L_ema` stays at the honest depth.** The warm-up seeds `L_ema` from the bucket highs `lhi` (`warm_step`, observe.rs:648-701), and the keeper's crank keeps those at H. After that, `steady_step` clamps `lobs` between `llo` and `lhi` (observe.rs:619-623), which freezes `L_ema` near H.
- **The guard never clears.** It clears only when `L_ema <= 1.01·L_mlo` (observe.rs:553-565, 703-712). With `L_mlo = D` and `L_ema` near H, the attacker can hold it set indefinitely by wrapping 4 of every 8 seconds from the warm-up on.
- **Nothing stops the liquidation.** In `liquidate`, the spot leg is judged at `l_spot = D` (liquidate.rs:351-357). The only post-change gate is `ema_warm` (liquidate.rs:569), and the keeper's own code says "the guard gates nothing" (services/keeper/src/decide.rs:222).
- **The exit bound is met.** A Raydium adoption sets `L_slow = min(L_slow, D)` (observe.rs:937-938), so `L_b = D` (bounds.rs:106-108). B̂_ref and B̂_live are then both priced at D.

The result: the FITS-2 (a) protection does not hold while the guard is set. ECON §5.5 says "a withdrawal lowers L_live but not L_ema'". Under the guard that is false, because `L_mlo` drops without any attacker-only seconds. The regression test `fits2_a_*` (freeze.rs:2198) does not catch this. It runs on a listed market whose guard clears at the gate after 13 s of honest cranks.

What limits it:
1. **Both legs must hold.** Liquidation needs the spot leg AND the EMA leg (liquidate.rs:306-308). The EMA leg reads the ring's cached values at `L_ema` near H, which the attacker cannot drag down. So a position that is healthy on the EMA leg cannot be forced. Only the FITS-2 (5b)(v) spike-and-retreat band is exposed: there `P_ema` lags above the robust spot `P_rs`, and the honest spot leg would block the liquidation. The sims put this at about 2.01–2.07× against a 2.078× threshold.
2. **Narrow preconditions.** It needs a restart (adoption, listing, graduation or PumpSwap price start). The attacker must hold the pool's unlocked LP (not possible on λ≈1 pools) and keep wrapping from the warm-up onward.
3. **Inside the accepted KI-23 bound.** Suppose the same LP instead withdrew for good at the restart. All warm-up highs would be D, so `L_ema = D` and the guard clears. The spot leg would be at D, the EMA leg at D (which makes liquidation easier, not harder), and `L_b = D`. The honest keeper would then force the same liquidations, apart from differences in price path. The attacker only saves keeping its capital out of the pool. Lenders are made whole; the borrower pays the penalty plus residual 3's overpay of about `(1/λ−1)·q/x`.

In short, this is a cheaper route into the accepted FITX-1 class, and it contradicts the stated claim that nothing is forced while the guard is set. Severity: Low.

verdicts.reason:
The code path is real. The impact is much smaller than "force-liquidates a healthy position" suggests.

How the attack works:
- An unlocked-LP holder wraps its crank as [withdraw, crank, deposit]. `record` keeps the lowest liquidity seen in each second (`llo = min`, observe.rs:466). So a wrapped sample lowers that second's low even when the keeper also observes that second; an honest observation cannot raise a low.
- `ring_liq_lower_median` takes index 3 of the 8 sorted lows (observe.rs:732-748). Four wrapped seconds out of every 8 therefore set `L_mlo` to the drained depth D.
- The guard clears only when `L_ema·10^4 <= L_mlo·10_100` (observe.rs:553-565, 705-711). The same wraps keep it from clearing for any λ below 0.99. The attacker has to start inside the 8-second warm-up and then keep it up at about 0.5 tx/s, which costs almost nothing.
- While the guard is set, `guarded_ema_liquidity` returns `min(L_ema, L_mlo)` = D (bounds.rs:117-122), so `spot_liquidity` = `max(L_live, D)` (bounds.rs:156-158). Inside the bundle `L_live` is D as well (liquidate.rs:351-357). This is the pre-#101 spot leg again.
- The exit bound does not block it:
  - On Raydium, adoption sets `L_slow <= D` (observe.rs:926-930). While the guard is set, `L_slow` takes in `min(lobs, L_mlo)` (observe.rs:625). So `L_b` ends up at D (bounds.rs:106-108) and the drained buyback stays within `max_in`.
  - On PumpSwap the cap is D itself.

What limits the impact:
1. `lobs = clamp(L_ema, llo, lhi)` (observe.rs:620), and the keeper covers every second while the guard is set. So `L_ema` stays near the honest depth H, and the EMA leg is judged at H. The attack only adds liquidations where the EMA leg is already true at H and P_rs < P_ema: ECON §12.12 (5b)(v), a spike followed by a retreat. In the sims that is a band just under the honest threshold: 2.01–2.07× against 2.078× (up to 3.3% in price) and 1.98–2.03× against 2.039× (up to 4.9%).
2. Cost to the borrower per forced liquidation:
   - the penalty: 0.64–1.00 SOL on the fork's FITX-1 reproducer positions, 30% of it to the attacker as keeper;
   - an overpay of at most about (1/λ−1)·q/x of B (+4.04%, 1.24 SOL in the sim);
   - the recovery the position would have made.
   Lenders are whole.
3. It needs a venue restart and an attacker who owns unlocked LP.
   - On a graduated PumpSwap pool the attacker must supply the extra depth itself, so H is just D plus its own deposit. With an exogenous price path, the positions it can force are ones that would be liquidated anyway without the attacker.
   - On Raydium, every forced liquidation is one the same LP could cause by withdrawing for good. That is the bound the owner accepted for FITX-1 (KI-23, 2026-09-29).
   - FITX-1 already works in steady state, with no restart needed. With a genuine hold of about 25 s or more it forces a superset of these positions.
   So the new exposure on top of the accepted residuals is small.

Why it still counts: the docs say this cannot happen. ECON.md:3423 (residual 3) and ARCHITECTURE.md:909 describe this exact setup (wrap at least 4 of the 8 warm-up seconds and at least 4 of every 8 after). They then claim "With the guard set it forces no exit (the reference and the seed read the honest lows)" and limit the harm to overpay. The #101 sims backing "nothing forced" (5b) ran with no switch and the guard clear; they never tested the spot leg's L_mlo floor while the guard is set. KI-20's stated limit is therefore exceeded, though the impact stays within KI-23's envelope. Of the report's two fixes, Option B (`min(L_ema, L_mhi)`) keeps the deposit-push protection; Option A drops it.

That statement is wrong for the spike-and-retreat case. The forced liquidations are covered by the bound of KI-23 / FITX-1 (residual 10, ECONOMICS.md:3430), which the owner accepted: they force only what the LP's withdrawal for good would force.
